heading: Issues of Edward's age
summary: Edward's minority created serious concerns about faction, regency and the stability of government.
facts: Henry had issued his Third Act of Succession in 1543. This confirmed that if Edward died without heirs the throne would pass to Mary and then Elizabeth.
The religious and factional struggles of the latter years of Henry's reign had left a divided council between the reformists and the conservatives.

When Edward became King in January 1547 there were serious concerns about his age. He was only nine when he came to the throne. It was feared that a regent might be appointed, that Edward wouldn't be able to control faction within the Council, and that the image of monarchy as a strong, divine power would be challenged by the image of a child.
Previous minorities had ended badly. In 1483 Richard III had seized power during his nephew's minority, and the young princes disappeared in the Tower.

Henry, fearing the negative influence of a single regent, instructed in his will that a Regency Council of 16 members should be formed, balanced between the reformists such as Seymour and conservatives led by Gardiner and Norfolk.
However in the last year of Henry's life Gardiner and Norfolk's fall from grace in 1546 meant the Council was no longer balanced, but weighted in favour of the reformists.

Following Henry's death Seymour and Paget conspired using the dry stamp and the 'unfulfilled gifts' clause of Henry's will to increase their power. Seymour was made Duke of Somerset, Lord Protector and predominant figure on the new Regency Council.

heading: The Regency Council
summary: Somerset used his position as Lord Protector to accumulate power, creating the factional tensions that would lead to his fall.
facts: Faction in government is not inevitably a destabilising force for monarchs. Other Tudor monarchs encouraged faction to ensure their ministers competed for their loyalty.
However, faction in the reign of a minor was more dangerous as there was no authority to control it. Factional disputes could spill over into rebellion or civil war.

Factions on the Council were initially defined in terms of religion: reformists and conservatives. Key reformers included Somerset and John Dudley, Earl of Warwick. Key conservatives included Thomas Wriothesley, Earl of Southampton.
The reformist faction, led by Somerset, dominated the Regency Council by 1547. He gave positions to supporters like his brother Thomas Seymour, who he later executed for treason.
As Lord Protector he was able to use the position to increase his personal wealth and power, which resulted in criticism from opponents and even former supporters.

heading: Somerset's fall
summary: Somerset's arrogance and the unrest of 1549 created an Anti-Somerset faction that forced his arrest and eventual execution.
facts: Somerset's arrogant and dominating leadership created a new faction: the Anti-Somerset faction. This was a combination of reformers and conservatives including Warwick, Wriothesley and Paget, the man who had helped Somerset's rise to power.
They also feared Somerset's apparent sympathy for the commoners and the problem of enclosure. They believed this sympathy had encouraged the unrest of the summer of 1549.
Edward himself disliked Somerset's control as he was allowed no influence at all.
The unrest of 1549 weakened Somerset's hold of power as many in the Council blamed his policies. Several, including Paget, wrote to Somerset criticising his leadership.

Feeling threatened, Somerset took possession of Edward and on the 5th October issued a general summons for all loyal subjects to defend the King and himself against the Council. This was seen as inciting revolt.
On the 6th Somerset retreated to Windsor Castle but was forced to surrender to the Council when the King turned against him, declaring he was being kept a prisoner by Somerset. Somerset was arrested.

heading: The rise of Northumberland
summary: Northumberland filled the power vacuum after Somerset's fall, securing his position by allying with the reformists and fabricating charges against Somerset.
facts: Following Somerset's fall there was a power vacuum on the Regency Council. Warwick's role in the defeat of both the Western and Kett's rebellions had made him politically indispensable — he was seen as a strong leader who could restore order.

Facing opposition from conservatives including the Earls of Arundel and Southampton, Warwick allied himself with the reformist faction and committed to further religious reform — becoming Lord President of the Council in 1550 and Duke of Northumberland.

He released Somerset and restored him to the Council in the hope he would use his influence to stabilise the regime — but when this failed, Somerset was arrested again and executed for treason in January 1552.
The evidence suggests the accusations of treason against Somerset were fabricated — Northumberland needed to remove the one figure who could plausibly challenge his dominance of the Council.

Northumberland's methods showed how dangerous minority rule was — without a strong monarch, the most ruthless faction could dominate government and eliminate opponents under cover of law. Edward himself was becoming more active in government by 1552–53, aged 14–15.

Northumberland promoted rapid Protestant reform under Stage 3 — the Second Book of Common Prayer (1552) and Forty-Two Articles — partly out of genuine conviction but also to cement his alliance with the reformist faction.

heading: The Devise for the Succession
summary: Edward and Northumberland attempted to exclude Mary from the succession by naming Lady Jane Grey as heir, but Mary's popular support ensured her triumph.
facts: In early 1553 Edward VI's health began to decline causing anxiety about the succession. Edward himself was concerned for the survival of the radical Protestant changes he so valued.
Mary was a committed Catholic and had maintained her faith throughout Edward's reign. Even Edward's personal appeals could not move her.
Northumberland was concerned for his own power. He knew that his role in government would lead to his fall from power when Mary came to the throne.

The Devise for the Succession was written naming the future male children of Jane Grey as Edward's heir. To preserve his power, Northumberland married his son Guildford Dudley to Jane Grey, hoping to control the heir. However, Edward's illness progressed rapidly before Jane Grey had children. In his own hand Edward crossed out 'male heirs' and named Jane Grey as his heir before his death.
Edward died on 6th July 1553. His death was kept quiet for 2 days whilst prominent nobles were pressured to sign the Devise.

Mary acted quickly. She had a significant power base in East Anglia and quickly dispatched riders to proclaim herself Queen. The Council proclaimed Jane on the 10th, after Mary's proclamation on the 9th.

Mary raised a large force of supporters. Northumberland left London to face Mary but on the way many of his army deserted him and the Councillors who had been forced to support the Devise broke ranks. Northumberland retreated to Cambridge and accepted Mary was queen on the 19th.

Mary triumphantly entered London to rousing support. She released Gardiner and Norfolk from jail and showed leniency towards many who opposed her. However, Northumberland, Lady Jane Grey and Guildford Dudley were all later executed.

heading: Issues of Mary's gender
summary: Mary's accession as the first Queen regnant raised deep concerns about female rule, though the willingness to make Jane Grey queen shows religion mattered more than gender.
facts: Mary was the first Queen to rule England in her own right.
In the 12th century, Matilda, daughter of Henry I, was named as heir to the throne. Following Henry's death there was a civil war as many nobles refused to accept Matilda.
Henry VIII's determination to gain a male heir shows the anxieties of leaving the realm to a female ruler.
Many believed female rulers would not be able to control powerful men in their government, lead soldiers into battle or display the power and strength that a monarch needed to epitomise.

Radical Protestants viewed female rulers as unnatural. John Knox wrote The First Blast of the Trumpet Against the Monstrous Regiment of Women in 1558, comparing female rulers to the 'blind leading those who can see'.
However, the willingness of Edward and Northumberland to make Jane Grey queen suggests issues of gender were seen as less important compared to religion.

heading: Mary's marriage
summary: Mary's marriage to Philip of Spain was carefully managed by treaty but ultimately ended unhappily, contributing to rebellion and foreign entanglement.
facts: Mary needed to marry to create an heir to ensure the longevity of her Catholic restoration. However, issues were raised about the suitor.

If Mary married an English noble this would lead to division and faction within court and Council. If Mary married a foreign prince this could lead to an unpopular influx of foreigners and England's entanglement in foreign wars.

Two major candidates emerged: Edward Courtenay, Earl of Devon, championed by Stephen Gardiner; and Philip of Spain, championed by Paget and Mary's personal choice. Philip would bring powerful diplomatic alliances as his father Charles V was Holy Roman Emperor and King of Spain. However, it risked a xenophobic popular reaction.

Fearing a negative reaction, a treaty was agreed by the Spanish representatives and Parliament to avoid instability. It was agreed that: Philip would be named King but have no power in his own right; no Spaniards would be granted offices or lands in England; after Mary's death Philip would have no claim to the throne; England would not be entangled in Spain's wars.
Despite reassurances, Wyatt's rebellion broke out in January 1554, ostensibly in reaction to the marriage to Philip.
Ultimately, the marriage ended unhappily. After Mary's phantom pregnancy, Philip rarely spent any time in England. When Mary died Philip commented he felt 'a reasonable regret'.

heading: Marian faction
summary: Mary streamlined her Council and dominated it through three key figures, though divisions between Gardiner and Pole over the pace of restoration created short-lived friction.
facts: One of the key criticisms of female rulers was that they would not be able to control the male ministers in their government, leading to damaging factional struggles and the collapse of government.

Mary was keen to ensure an efficient and streamlined administration and so made adjustments to the Council. 'Casual councillors' were excluded from key committees in 1554. In 1555 Mary established an 'inner council' so only her most valued advisors were present.

Mary's Council was dominated by three key figures: Stephen Gardiner, Bishop of Winchester, a long standing committed Catholic and cautious realist; William Paget, an eminent political survivor and exceptional administrator who was not committed to religious change; Cardinal Reginald Pole, a fiercely zealous Catholic who had gone into exile during the reign of Henry VIII.
One key division in the Council was over Mary's potential suitors. Gardiner championed the Earl of Devon; Paget championed Philip, knowing he was Mary's preferred choice.

Pole's return in 1554 brought dispute between Gardiner and Pole over the pace and methods of the restoration of Catholicism. Gardiner stressed caution and persuasion whereas Pole favoured dramatic change backed up by persecution.

However these struggles were minor and short lived. Gardiner's death in 1555 ensured Pole's methods won out. For the majority of Mary's reign the Council worked effectively and carried out her wishes.

heading: Succession in 1558
summary: Mary died having failed to produce an heir, leaving England weakened by debt and war, and Elizabeth faced an immediate Catholic challenge to her legitimacy.
facts: Mary died on 17th November 1558. Cardinal Pole died on the same day, leaving the Church of England without an Archbishop of Canterbury.
Mary had failed to produce an heir. Her phantom pregnancy in 1555 had raised hopes that were quickly dashed, and Philip had largely abandoned England after 1555.
England had also suffered the humiliation of losing Calais in 1558, the last English territory in France, as a consequence of Mary's decision to join Spain's war against France.

The succession passed peacefully to Elizabeth. Philip of Spain, despite having the power to press a claim, chose not to. He recognised Elizabeth as Queen, preferring a Protestant England to a France-aligned Catholic one.

However many Catholics viewed Elizabeth as illegitimate, due to the Pope's refusal to grant Henry VIII's divorce from Catherine of Aragon. Instead they believed Mary, Queen of Scots was the true Queen of England. Mary was a Catholic monarch, married to the French Dauphin Francis. King Henry II of France presented Mary as the true queen of England, a figure unifying Scotland, France and England against Elizabeth.
Elizabeth therefore inherited not just a country divided by religion, weakened by war and debt, but an immediate Catholic challenge to the legitimacy of her rule.

heading: Religious inheritance
summary: Henry VIII's Reformation was incomplete and ambiguous, leaving England with a divided Church and a population largely unfamiliar with Protestant doctrine.
facts: Despite Henry VIII's Break from Rome in 1534, Henry never truly embraced Protestantism — he only embraced Protestant changes that would bring him money and power, most notably the Dissolution of the Monasteries (1536–41).

The 1539 Act of Six Articles confirmed Catholic doctrine including Transubstantiation, clerical celibacy, private masses and auricular confession — England was doctrinally Catholic despite the break with Rome.

The majority of the country, outside London and East Anglia, likely did not fully understand the differences between Catholicism and Protestantism and just wanted to worship as their ancestors had done for a millennium.

Henry left a divided council — Gardiner and Norfolk's fall from grace in 1546 meant it was already weighted in favour of the reformists before Edward came to the throne, making further Protestant reform likely.

The repeal of the Act of Six Articles under Somerset in 1547 opened the door to radical Protestant preaching. Calvinism, Zwinglism and Lutheranism were all being preached, creating confusion about what the official doctrine actually was.

The Dissolution of the Monasteries had removed a key source of Catholic charitable provision and community — but it had also created a powerful vested interest among the gentry who had bought monastic land and would resist any Catholic restoration that threatened their property.

heading: Edward's Reformation: destruction
summary: The first stage of the Edwardian Reformation in 1547 focused on dismantling the Catholic Church before a new settlement could be imposed.
facts: The leading architects of radical change, Archbishop Cranmer and Somerset, had to act slowly. Before they could install their new religion, the old had to be destroyed.

Repeal of the Six Articles removed the Catholic doctrine set out by Henry.
Repeal of the Treason Act meant it was no longer treason to preach dissenting religious views.
Dissolution of the Chantries that were seen as superstitious forms of Catholic worship. Also brought in a lot of revenue and land for the Crown.

heading: Edward's Reformation: formulation
summary: The second and third stages of the Edwardian Reformation attempted to fill the religious vacuum with a new Protestant settlement, culminating in the explicitly Calvinist Second Book of Common Prayer.
facts: Stage 2 – Limbo, 1548–49: The repeal of the Treason Laws opened up a Pandora's Box of new radical ideas. Various versions of radical Protestantism were being preached including Calvinism, Zwinglism and Lutheranism.

In December 1548, Cranmer published his First Book of Common Prayer. This was enforced nationwide in the First Act of Uniformity. It was a compromise between the old and the new and did not please anyone. Notably it was extremely vague on the stance on Holy Communion. This Prayer Book prompted rebellion in the West Country.

Stage 3 – Formulation, 1550–53: Following Northumberland's rise the pace of religious reform increased. A new ordinal was introduced in 1550, allowing leading Catholic clergy to be deprived of their positions and replaced with Protestants.

In 1552, Cranmer published the Second Book of Common Prayer, enforced by the second Act of Uniformity. This was much more radical and unambiguous than the first. It removed all Catholic practices, and confirmed Calvin's doctrine that Communion was purely symbolic.
In 1552, the Forty-Two Articles, outlining the key doctrines of Edward's Church, were drawn up. Edward's death in 1553 ensured these Articles were never passed by Parliament.
Nevertheless, by 1553, de jure England was a Protestant country.

heading: De facto change under Edward
summary: Despite the legal changes, the Edwardian Reformation made limited impact on actual religious practice in most of England beyond London and the south-east.
facts: Just because de jure England was Protestant does not mean de facto this was true nationally.
Edward's rule lasted six years. In an age when ideas spread slowly this was a small amount of time to upend 1,000 years of Catholic worship.
Bishop Hooper's visitations around his diocese of Gloucester found that of 311 clergymen, 171 were unable to repeat the Ten Commandments and 40 could not find the Lord's Prayer.
The repeated efforts to remove icons and the visitations prove the changes were hard to enforce.
Evidence from people's wills shows little support for the changes except in London, south-east and East Anglia – the areas closest to the centre of power.
There was open rebellion against Protestantism in the West Country.

Many people simply conformed because they were told they had to. The rapid restoration of Catholicism under Mary might suggest that traditional religion still retained its popularity, making Mary's task that much easier.

heading: Mary's religious aims
summary: Mary aimed to restore England to full Papal authority and Catholic practice, though her advisors cautioned against moving too quickly.
facts: Mary's religious aims were: to undo religious changes made since 1529, including restoring Papal authority, Catholic practices and belief in transubstantiation, and monasteries that had been dissolved; to secure a long-term future for Catholicism by marrying and having children; to ensure the Catholic religion is abided by across the country.

Mary's advisors were concerned about the feasibility of some of these aims. Gardiner was uncertain about restoring papal authority and the Imperial ambassador, Simon Renard, expressed concerns about trying to restore former monastic property.
Even Charles V and the pope, Julius III, were concerned that Mary would proceed too quickly and provoke unrest that might even threaten her position as queen.
Parliament met in October 1553 but refused to repeal the Act of Supremacy, suggesting anti-Papal feeling. However it did pass the 1st Act of Repeal which restored the religious situation of 1547.
Mary used the royal prerogative to get rid of the Second Act of Uniformity and restore the Catholic Mass.

In April 1554 there was controversy in parliament over the issue of ex-monastic land. Landowning MPs who had benefited from the dissolution refused to reinstate the heresy laws until Mary had given them assurances regarding their land. In November Mary accepted ex-monastic land would be left. The heresy laws were then revived.

heading: The Marian burnings

heading: Socioeconomic causes of unrest
summary: A combination of population rise, debasement, enclosure and Spanish bullion created the Great Price Rise that drove poverty and social tension across the mid-Tudor period.
facts: Inflation had been occurring throughout the 16th century, but accelerated in the 1540s. Food prices had doubled since the start of the century.

Population rise – Malthusian Crisis: for the first time since the Black Death the population of England was rising. From 1525–1551 the population rose from 2.3 million to 3 million. Agricultural productivity was unable to keep pace and therefore the price of food rose.
Bad harvests were common. This was exacerbated by the end of the Medieval Warm Period and beginning of the Little Ice Age.

Debasement: in order to finance wars against France and Scotland in the early 1540s, Henry VIII's government had begun a policy of debasement. Debasement reduced confidence in the currency and so prices rose to compensate. Somerset continued debasement to fund the war against Scotland.

Enclosure began to pick up pace in the Tudor period due to the growing cloth market in the Netherlands. English wool was prized and so many gentry transformed their land from agriculture to livestock farming. This led to less food being produced, higher food prices, and increased unemployment.

Commonwealth men, not understanding the impact of the population rise or debasement, blamed the Great Price Rise on enclosure and greedy gentlemen. This added to the complaints that the gentry and merchant class regularly practiced rack renting and regrating to exploit the poor.

Spain's conquest of the New World meant that vast quantities of American gold and silver were being imported into Europe. This meant that across Europe the value of these metals decreased and so the value of coinage decreased, exacerbating price rises.

The Great Price Rise, combined with increasing demand for land, led to high levels of poverty and vagrancy. Fears over increases in vagrancy prompted the Vagrancy Act of 1547 which condemned vagrants to two years slavery for the first offence, and lifetime slavery for a second.

heading: Kett's Rebellion
summary: Kett's Rebellion of 1549 was the most serious of the year's widespread unrest, capturing Norwich before being crushed by Warwick at Dussindale.
facts: 1549 was a year of serious unrest across the country. Whilst the Kett and Western Rebellions were the largest, there were not the limits of the unrest. Like the Hydra of Greek mythology, cutting off one head, simply created two more. Over half the counties of England saw unrest.

The unrest began when a mob in Norfolk attacked the enclosures of John Flowerdew, a local gentleman. Flowerdew redirected the protest to Robert Kett, another gentleman who had also enclosed much land. Somehow Kett became the leader of this unrest. The rebels soon numbered 16,000.

Many of the rebels' demands were concerned with enclosure and high rents. However, there were also complaints about absent or uneducated clergy. Divisions were clear in Norwich as 6% owned 60% of the land.

16,000 rebels met in July 1549. They marched on Norwich – camped at Mousehold Heath. They then stormed Norwich. Kett ran a well-ordered camp – justice was administered to show they could maintain order.
Government sent over 14,000 troops. Earl Warwick came and massacred the rebels at Dussindale. 3,000 were killed. A further 49 of the leaders were executed for treason.

Reasons for failure: Warwick had 12,000 well-trained and experienced troops from the war with Scotland. Kett was not an experienced military leader. He abandoned his well-defended camp at Mousehold Heath to meet Warwick at Dussindale.

heading: The Western Rebellion
summary: The Western or Prayer Book Rebellion of 1549 was primarily a religious reaction to the First Book of Common Prayer, though economic grievances also played a role.
facts: A prelude to the unrest was the brutal murder of William Body in 1548. Body had been tasked by the government to supervise iconoclasm in Cornwall which was extremely unpopular.

There was also large opposition to the First Book of Common Prayer enforced in early 1549. Many wanted the return of the old Latin services. Partly because they did not follow the new religion and partly because many Cornishmen were more familiar with Latin than English.

The list of demands produced by the rebels are almost entirely occupied with halting religious change. However this is largely because the demands were drawn up by the local clergy who were literate. There is evidence that early demands excluded by the clergy included demands about high taxes and rents. At Bodmin the rebels would chant 'Kill all the gentlemen!'.

The rebels initially gathered to protest the Book of Common Prayer at Sampford Courtenay. Gentry were attacked at St Michael's Mount, Bodmin and Trematon Castle. Some of the rebels marched on Exeter and besieged the city.
After around a month, a government force of 8,000 led by Lord John Russell defeated the rebels at Sampford Courtenay. Over 3,000 were executed.

Failure: unlike the unrest in East Anglia, the Western Rebellion had no clear leadership. Different sections of the rebels attacked different targets. Like in East Anglia, there was limited military leadership.

How threatening? 1549 saw the most widespread unrest of the Tudor period. Over 25 counties saw significant unrest. However, at no point did either Kett's or the Western rebels attempt to march on London to force regime change.

heading: Wyatt's Rebellion: causes

facts: Mary's marriage to Philip of Spain led to concerns over a foreign marriage and that patronage would be given to the Spanish and that England would be dragged into the Habsburg's wars.

Religion: the rebellion began in Kent, a more Protestant area with trading links to Protestant Northern Europe. Many of the leaders were Protestant including Thomas Wyatt. Part of the plot was to replace Mary with Elizabeth who would defend Protestantism.

Many leaders of the rebellion, including Wyatt, had lost positions at court due to their faith. This was an attempt to regain their old power.

heading: Wyatt's Rebellion: consequences
summary: Wyatt's Rebellion failed due to the premature rising and Mary's decisive leadership, but its consequences shaped the rest of her reign.
facts: A plot developed between Wyatt, Sir James Croft, and Sir Peter Carew for a four-pronged attack from Devon, Leicestershire, the Welsh borders and Kent. Having been discovered, the rebels had to act immediately. Only Wyatt in Kent did. He raised 3,000 men and began to march on London.
A government force led by the Duke of Norfolk was sent to face the rebels. The government soldiers deserted Norfolk and joined Wyatt's men declaring 'We are all Englishmen!'.

Wyatt reached the gates of London. Mary stood resolutely and refused to flee the city. She gave an impassioned speech at Guildhall which secured the support of the Londoners who refused to open the city gates to Wyatt. The royal forces, supported by the Londoners, defeated Wyatt's rebellion.
Wyatt and the leaders were executed, and Elizabeth was imprisoned in the Tower.

Reasons for failure: the discovery of the plot meant the rebels were forced to rise in Winter. This meant fewer peasants were willing to join. Only one of the four forces rebelled as the other leaders got cold feet. Mary's strength and leadership ensured the rebellion was ultimately defeated.

Consequences: Lady Jane Grey and Guildford Dudley were executed. Elizabeth was imprisoned in the Tower, though released after Wyatt refused to implicate her under torture. Mary proceeded with the marriage to Philip.

heading: Religious pressures in 1558
summary: Elizabeth faced a complex set of domestic and international religious pressures in 1558 that shaped the nature of her Religious Settlement.
facts: c.800 leading Protestants had fled England at the start of Mary I's reign. In their exile they had based themselves in the Protestant hotspots of Zurich, Frankfurt and Geneva where many had become more radical, educated with the teachings of John Calvin or Huldrych Zwingli.
Calvinism and Zwinglism were threats to Elizabeth as they denied the need for an episcopacy in the Church. This extended to the monarch who was said to have no role in the Church.

Under Mary I's reign Catholicism had been restored to England by law. Even without this restoration, much of the English population had never left Catholicism. The powerful bishops Elizabeth inherited from Mary were all Catholics.

Due to the Pope's refusal to grant Henry VIII's divorce from Catherine of Aragon, many Catholics viewed Elizabeth as illegitimate and thus not the true Queen. Instead they believed Mary, Queen of Scots was the true Queen of England.

Elizabeth inherited from Mary a war with France and an alliance with Spain through Mary's marriage to Phillip. Spain and France were the two richest and most powerful countries in the world. They were both strongly Catholic.
Fortunately for Elizabeth the Habsburg-Valois rivalry meant they despised each other. Elizabeth's political future depended on this rivalry continuing.

heading: The Religious Settlement
summary: The Religious Settlement of 1559 established a deliberately ambiguous via media, designed to accommodate as many subjects as possible.
facts: The Act of Supremacy removed the Pope's authority over the English Church. Made Elizabeth Supreme Governor of the Church.
Elizabeth was in charge of a strict episcopal hierarchy consisting of Archbishops and Bishops. Mary's heresy laws were repealed – no more burnings.
Cranmer's 1552 Book of Common Prayer was used in all churches. However the most radical passage the 'Black Rubric' that explicitly denied transubstantiation was omitted.
During Holy Communion, wording from both the 1552 and the more conservative 1548 Prayer Books was used. This allowed an open interpretation of Transubstantiation or Consubstantiation.
Everyone must attend a licensed Church of England church on a Sunday. Those failing to do so would be guilty of recusancy and charged 1 shilling – average weekly wage of a labourer.

The Royal Injunctions: church taxes were to be paid to the Crown; the few small monasteries that Mary had managed to restore were dissolved again; the clergy were to wear distinctive vestments; music was encouraged at services and images were accepted; the clergy could marry.
Elizabeth described the settlement as Via Media 'the middle way'. It was designed to be an acceptable compromise for Catholics and radical Protestants that would cease the religious conflict.

heading: Getting the Settlement through Parliament
summary: The Settlement faced serious opposition in the House of Lords from Catholic bishops, requiring Elizabeth to use prorogation and compromise to get it passed.
facts: Elizabeth could not use proclamations or decrees to enact religious change. She needed to get it through parliament to give it legitimacy and make it enforceable.
This was not anticipated to be a problem. Neither Edward or Mary had encountered significant parliamentary opposition to their religious changes.

However in the 1559 parliament, the Catholic bishops and some Catholic lay nobles in the House of Lords showed they would oppose and alter the settlement. In particular making Elizabeth 'Head of the Church'.

Elizabeth in response, prorogued parliament over the Easter of 1559 to delay. Elizabeth arrested two of the more vocal critics the Bishops of Lincoln and Winchester for disobedience and compromised by adopting the title 'Supreme Governor' instead.
The Settlement then passed the House of Lords by a margin of just three votes. Elizabeth was then able to remove the Marian bishops when they refused to swear the Oath of Loyalty.

heading: The Puritan challenge: Parliament
summary: Puritan MPs attempted to push Elizabeth towards a more radical Protestant settlement through parliament, but Elizabeth consistently defended her royal prerogative over religious matters.
facts: The historian John Neale argued that a small but highly organised group of Puritan MPs — the 'Puritan Choir' — attempted to alter the Religious Settlement through Acts of Parliament. Later historians like Geoffrey Elton have questioned whether this group was as organised as Neale suggested.

Strickland's Proposals (1571): Puritan MP Walter Strickland attempted to alter the Book of Common Prayer to remove vestments, the ring in marriage and kneeling at communion. He was summoned before the Privy Council for infringing the Royal Prerogative and barred from Parliament.

Cope's Proposals (1586): Anthony Cope MP made an extremely radical 'bill and book' proposal that would have replaced the Book of Common Prayer with the Genevan Prayer Book and removed the episcopacy entirely. Cope and four supporters were sent to the Tower of London. The bill was defeated.

Peter Wentworth MP was a persistent champion of parliamentary freedom of speech. In 1566 his brother Paul challenged Elizabeth's restriction of parliamentary debate. In 1576 Peter compared Elizabeth's involvement in Parliament to 'the work of the devil' — the House of Commons itself sent him to the Tower.

Elizabeth consistently framed religious matters as part of the Royal Prerogative — beyond parliamentary competence. Puritan MPs were never able to force lasting change through Parliament, and Elizabeth's management of the Speaker and ability to prorogue meant she retained control.

Strickland's Proposals (1571): Puritan MP Walter Strickland attempted to alter the Book of Common Prayer to remove vestments, the ring in marriage and kneeling at communion. He was summoned before the Privy Council for infringing the Royal Prerogative and barred from Parliament.

Cope's Proposals (1586): Anthony Cope MP made an extremely radical 'bill and book' proposal that would have replaced the Book of Common Prayer with the Genevan Prayer Book and removed the episcopacy entirely. Cope and four supporters were sent to the Tower of London. The bill was defeated.

subheadings.label: Peter Wentworth and free speech
facts: Peter Wentworth MP was a persistent champion of parliamentary freedom of speech. In 1566 his brother Paul challenged Elizabeth's restriction of parliamentary debate. In 1576 Peter compared Elizabeth's involvement in Parliament to 'the work of the devil' — the House of Commons itself sent him to the Tower.

Elizabeth consistently framed religious matters as part of the Royal Prerogative — beyond parliamentary competence. Puritan MPs were never able to force lasting change through Parliament, and Elizabeth's management of the Speaker and ability to prorogue meant she retained control.

heading: The Puritan challenge: clergy and separatism
summary: Puritans challenged the settlement from within the Church through the Vestiarian Controversy, popular pamphlets, and ultimately separatist movements.
facts: The Vestiarian Controversy – Puritans despised the wearing of vestments as they signified clergy to be holy men separate to ordinary worshippers. The Archbishop of Canterbury, Matthew Parker, compromised in his 1566 Advertisements – he conceded that clergy could wear simply a 'comely surplice with long sleeves' at Communion. However, 37 Puritan clergymen who refused to accept Parker's compromise lost their jobs.

The 39 Articles – these articles were the central ordinances of the new Church of England. They had been initially agreed by the Convocation in 1563 however many were resisted by Puritans as they were not seen as radical enough. In 1571 it was conceded that clergy with reservations need not follow the ceremonial articles. However all clergy had to follow doctrinal articles.
Cambridge Presbyterian professor Thomas Cartwright gave a series of lectures in 1570 strongly denouncing the hierarchy in the Church. He lost his professorship and his freedom of speech.
Admonition to Parliament – in 1572 John Field and Thomas Wilcox penned a public criticism of parliament calling for the end of Church episcopacy.
Marprelate Tracts – series of Puritan pamphlets issued 1588-89 under the pseudonym of Martin Marprelate. Alienated many moderates with their vicious and provocative attacks on bishops.

Several Puritan groups attempted to establish an independent Puritan Church. 1581 Brownist Church led by Robert Browne in Norwich. 1590s a new Separatist movement was led by Henry Barrow and John Greenwood in London. The leaders were arrested and executed in 1593.
Puritanism survived through prophesyings and the classis movement as well as the protection of Privy Councillors like Leicester.

heading: Elizabeth's archbishops
summary: Elizabeth's three archbishops of Canterbury each shaped the Church's response to Puritanism in different ways, from Parker's compromise to Whitgift's repression.
facts: Matthew Parker (1559–75): Parker had previously been Anne Boleyn's chaplain. He had not gone into exile during Mary's reign and was not radicalised by Calvinism or Zwinglism. He defended the Settlement by overseeing the 39 Articles at the Convocation of 1563 — resisting Puritan attempts by a single vote — and publishing his 1566 Advertisements to compromise on vestments.

Edmund Grindal (1575–83): unlike Parker, Grindal was a former Marian exile who was sympathetic to Puritan concerns. He came into conflict with Elizabeth over prophesyings (meetings of clergy to discuss theology). When Elizabeth ordered him to suppress them in 1576, he refused, writing a 6,000-word letter defending prophesyings. Elizabeth suspended him in 1577 and he remained under house arrest until his death.

John Whitgift (1583–1604): after her conflict with Grindal, Elizabeth needed a loyal Archbishop. Whitgift used the Court of High Commission to root out non-conformists and issued the Three Articles as a test — clergy had to swear that Elizabeth had sovereignty over all Church matters, that the Book of Common Prayer was the only one to be used, and that the 39 Articles were agreeable to God.

Around 300 Puritan clergy were removed by Whitgift's methods. Cecil initially criticised the Three Articles as 'too inquisitorial'. But Whitgift showed that determined repression could contain though not eliminate the Puritan challenge.

Elizabeth supported Whitgift strongly throughout his archiepiscopacy — she died holding his hand in 1603. The contrast between Grindal's defiance and Whitgift's loyalty illustrates Elizabeth's insistence on control of the Church as part of her Royal Prerogative.

heading: Mary Queen of Scots and the Rising of the North
summary: The arrival of Mary Queen of Scots in 1568 transformed the Catholic threat, providing a figurehead for plots and triggering the Rising of the North in 1569.
facts: When Mary returned to Scotland in 1561 she found a country ruled by the Protestant Lords. Mary's second husband, Lord Darnley, was murdered in 1567 — Mary was widely suspected of involvement. She subsequently married the chief suspect, the Earl of Bothwell. This led the Protestant Lords to force her abdication in 1567 and imprisonment.

Mary escaped and fled to northern England in 1568, seeking Elizabeth's support. Elizabeth placed her under house arrest — Mary was too dangerous to release (a Catholic claimant to the English throne) but too politically sensitive to return to Scotland.

Mary was a real danger to Elizabeth as she was Elizabeth's cousin and next in line. Many English Catholics viewed Mary as the true Queen of England. Her arrival in the highly Catholic North provided a figurehead around which Catholic plots would ferment.

A plot to marry Mary to the powerful Duke of Norfolk to strengthen her claim to the English throne was uncovered. The Catholic northern earls of Northumberland and Westmoreland launched an uprising — the Rising of the North. The rebels captured Durham and held Catholic Latin mass in the Cathedral.

No other Catholic nobility answered the summons to rebel. A royal army marched north and the rebels fled without fighting a major battle. Elizabeth executed 450 rebels — a deliberately exemplary punishment. Norfolk was released but later executed in 1572 for the Ridolfi Plot.

In 1570, Pope Pius V issued his Papal bull Regnans in Excelsis excommunicating Elizabeth — Catholics were now absolved of any loyalty to her. This transformed the Catholic threat from passive non-conformity to active potential treachery, and dramatically escalated the government's legislative response.

heading: The Catholic plots
summary: A series of Catholic plots against Elizabeth culminated in the Babington Plot, which provided the evidence needed to execute Mary Queen of Scots.
facts: 1571 – The Ridolfi Plot: following Elizabeth's excommunication, Catholic Italian banker Ridolfi plotted with the Pope, Philip II of Spain and the Duke of Norfolk to marry Mary to Norfolk and provoke a Catholic uprising. heading: Seminary priests and Jesuits
summary: The arrival of seminary priests from Douai and Jesuits from Rome from the 1570s revitalised English Catholicism and dramatically escalated the government's response.
facts: Elizabeth's hope that the lack of trained Catholic priests would lead to Catholicism dying out was countered by William Allen's 'English College' at Douai in France, founded in 1568. Allen trained seminary priests specifically to return to England and minister secretly to English Catholics.

The first Seminary Priests trained by Allen arrived in 1574. By 1585, 279 Seminary Priests had travelled to England. From the 1580s the Jesuits also arrived — in total around 650 Jesuits or seminary priests were active in England, sheltered by Catholic gentry in priest holes.

The most famous Jesuit was Edmund Campion, who arrived in 1580. He was captured in 1581, tortured and executed — his death became a cause célèbre among English Catholics. Robert Parsons was another leading Jesuit who escaped to the Continent and continued organising the mission.

Government response: 1571 — treason to possess or distribute a copy of the Papal Bull. 1581 — Parliament increased recusancy fines to £20 a month; converting someone to Catholicism was made treason. 1585 — all Catholic priests expelled from England; harbouring a priest made punishable by death.

133 seminary priests and Jesuits were executed as a result of the 1585 legislation. The arrival of priests revitalised English Catholicism — but also gave the government justification for treating all Catholics as potential traitors.

Parliament repeatedly pushed for Mary QoS's execution in 1572, 1585 and 1586. The combined pressure of the Lords, Commons and Privy Council following the Babington Plot finally forced Elizabeth's hand — Mary was executed in February 1587.

heading: Problems facing the Catholics
summary: Despite the plots and priests, English Catholics faced overwhelming obstacles that limited the threat they posed to Elizabeth's settlement.
facts: Elizabeth's tolerance: for many English Catholics the Religious Settlement of 1559 was better than they expected. The heresy laws were repealed and the sole punishment was a recusancy fine of 1 shilling. Elizabeth's refusal to create martyrs meant that for the majority of Catholics there was no need to overtly oppose the settlement.
The Pope's 1570 excommunication was in many ways too little, too late. It came after the English had had 11 years to get used to the Settlement and after the Northern Rising had been crushed.

The Habsburg-Valois rivalry between the Spanish and French crowns prevented the great Catholic powers working together. 1566-1648 Spain was attempting to suppress the Protestant Dutch Revolt. 1562-98 the French Wars of Religion raged between the Catholic League and the Huguenots.
The failure of the Spanish Armada in 1588 was a major propaganda boost for Elizabeth and Protestantism.

Elizabeth's longevity: both Edward VI and Mary I were unable to cement their religious changes during their short reigns. Elizabeth was on the throne for 45 years. During her long reign the Catholic establishment from Mary's reign died out and the new generation of gentry, nobility and clergy all grew up under Elizabeth's settlement.

heading: Overview of national government
summary: Elizabethan government operated through a triangle of monarch, Privy Council and Parliament, with the monarch retaining supreme authority through the royal prerogative.
facts: The monarch was believed to derive their power directly from God. All legislation had to be approved by the monarch's Royal Assent. Unlike today, the monarch had every right to veto legislation they did not approve of.
The monarch could issue Royal proclamations that were expected to be followed, and had the power to call, prorogue, and dissolve parliament at will.
The Royal Prerogative were the issues that only the monarch had the right to decide upon. They included: religion, the succession, and foreign policy.

The Privy Council was the council of the monarch's most important advisors. Maximum of 20 members. Met several times a week. Key figures including the Secretary of State and Lord Treasurer. Dominated for most of the reign by William Cecil.

Parliament could pass legislation which was more permanent and enforceable than a proclamation. The monarch needed the approval of parliament to gain taxation. Called ten times during Elizabeth's reign.

MPs in the House of Commons tended to be members of the gentry. House of Lords included the Lords Temporal (nobility) and Lords Spiritual (bishops). Legislation had to be approved by both houses before being sent for Royal Assent.

heading: Key figures on the Privy Council
summary: Elizabeth's most important councillors dominated government throughout her reign, with Cecil providing administrative stability and Walsingham intelligence and security.
facts: William Cecil (Lord Burghley from 1571): Cecil was Elizabeth's principal advisor until his death in 1598. He was Secretary of State until 1572, then Lord Treasurer. Extremely hard-working and loyal, he helped draft the Religious Settlement, managed Elizabeth's correspondence, created an intelligence service and ran the Privy Council. By nature cautious and pragmatic.

Robert Dudley (Earl of Leicester from 1564): Dudley was Elizabeth's favourite — they had been imprisoned together in the Tower under Mary. Promoted more for personality than political skill — tall, handsome, charismatic. His wife Amy Robsart died in mysterious circumstances in 1560. A devout Puritan who championed military intervention to protect Protestants abroad.

Sir Francis Walsingham: a protégé of Cecil with a similar loyalty to Elizabeth and equal hostility to Mary Queen of Scots. Took over the intelligence service and Secretary of State in 1573. A devout Puritan who uncovered the Throckmorton and Babington Plots.

Thomas Howard, Duke of Norfolk: the most senior nobleman in England and the only Duke. Raised Protestant but with strong Catholic familial links. Initially a member of the Privy Council but executed in 1572 for his involvement in the Ridolfi Plot.

Robert Devereux, Earl of Essex: rose to favour in the 1590s as Leicester's godson. Charming, impulsive and popular but lacking political judgement. Raised to the Privy Council in 1593 but fell from grace over Ireland in 1599. His 1601 rebellion against Cecil's dominance failed immediately — executed for treason.

Sir Robert Cecil: son of William Cecil, rose to Secretary of State in 1596 whilst Essex was at Cadiz. Cautious and systematic like his father. From 1601 onwards dominated government unopposed and managed the smooth transition to James I in 1603.

heading: Elizabeth's management of faction
summary: Elizabeth deliberately encouraged factional competition among her councillors, using personal charm and calculated delay to prevent any single minister from dominating.
facts: Elizabeth stayed aloof of faction, and in fact encouraged such disputes to get a wider debate on certain issues. By taking her time before making decisions, Elizabeth did not show favour to any particular faction and was not easily swayed by her Councillors.
Elizabeth used her gender to manage loyalty as courtiers and Councillors would compete for her affection.

1565-66, Leicester came into dispute with a faction led by Norfolk and his cousin the Earl of Sussex. Norfolk accused Leicester of having murdered Amy Robsart in order to marry Elizabeth. The factions wore identifying ribbons at court. Elizabeth ended the dispute by making it clear she would not marry Leicester.

1578-85, The Dutch Revolt divided the Council. Leicester and Walsingham, as devout Puritans, urged direct intervention to support the Dutch rebels. The more watchful Burghley urged caution for fear of risking Spanish retaliation and an expensive and threatening war.

Mary, Queen of Scots was an issue that united the Council against Elizabeth. Repeatedly the Council petitioned Elizabeth to execute Mary. They agreed the Bond of Association to force the matter in 1584.

heading: Managing Parliament
summary: Elizabeth used a range of tools to manage Parliament, from prorogation and the royal veto to controlling the Speaker and exploiting the Privy Council's influence.
facts: If Elizabeth disapproved of a particular batch of MPs in a Parliament she could dissolve the parliament. Then when she called a new Parliament, new MPs would be elected.

Alternatively Elizabeth could prorogue parliament which would suspend the parliament for as long as she liked. During the suspension she or her Privy Council could put pressure on MPs to change their position.
The Privy Council were expected to promote Elizabeth's wishes in Parliament. Many Councillors were prominent politicians who dominated Parliamentary business.
Elizabeth and the Privy Council influenced the choice of Speaker of the House who controlled debates, chose who could speak and thus could control the Commons.
If a bill that Elizabeth disapproved of did manage to pass both Houses of Parliament, Elizabeth could use her Royal Veto to reject the proposed law.

As a last resort, Elizabeth had the ability to arrest MPs who directly challenged her prerogative as traitors. However such an aggressive use of royal power could potentially increase parliamentary opposition.

summary: Elizabeth's refusal to marry or name a successor was a calculated political strategy, though it created serious constitutional uncertainty and fuelled factional conflict.
facts: It was expected that Elizabeth would marry and produce an heir. An unclear succession following a monarch's death had previously led to anarchy, civil war and, in Elizabeth's lifetime, the Lady Jane Grey affair.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs
heading: Financial situation in 1558
summary: Elizabeth inherited a debt of £227,000 from Mary's reign but, with the help of capable administrators, quickly stabilised the finances and paid off the debt by 1576.
facts: When Elizabeth acceded to the throne in 1558, the English Crown had debts of £227,000 left over from Mary's involvement in the war with France. This debt was largely owed to the Antwerp Exchange and came with an interest rate of 14%.

Mary had introduced some reforms to make financial administration more efficient; most notable the revised Book of Rates which determined customs duties. Mary gave greater import to the Exchequer which now collected roughly three-quarters of Crown revenue.

Sir Thomas Gresham was a highly perceptive financier who identified three major problems facing Elizabeth's finances: debasement of the coinage that had begun under Henry VIII; the cost of war and the necessary but damaging loans needed to fund it; and the control the Hanseatic League enjoyed over the export market.

Gresham's primary advice to Elizabeth was to in peacetime maintain an excellent credit rating by swiftly repaying existing debt, and avoiding taking loans. In 1565 Gresham founded the Royal Exchange as a London equivalent to the Antwerp Exchange.

Elizabeth quickly and effectively removed the Marian debt. By 1576 the Chancellor of the Exchequer informed parliament that the Marian debt had been removed. By 1584 Elizabeth had accrued a surplus of £300,000. She achieved this by not indulging in the excessive lifestyle of her father, avoiding lavish building projects, going on 'progress' each summer, and avoiding war at all cost.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs
heading: Methods of raising income
summary: Elizabeth relied primarily on ordinary revenue in the first half of her reign, but the war with Spain from 1585 forced increasing dependence on parliamentary taxation.
facts: Ordinary revenue was the income that the Crown would receive by default, every year. Examples included: revenue from the rent of Crown lands, Customs Duties, profits from justice, and Church revenue – for example First Fruits and Tenths.

Extraordinary revenue was income that the Crown could gain in addition to ordinary revenue in times of need. Parliamentary grants of subsidies could be requested. Loans could be acquired forcibly from wealthy nobles or at high interest rates from financial centres.

Crown Lands: Elizabeth increased her annual revenues from Crown lands from £86,000 to £111,000. However Elizabeth sold a significant portion of Crown Lands which, over her reign, brought an income of £600,000 but depleted the long-term potential for Crown income.

Customs Duties: Mary's revision of the Book of Rates in 1558 provided an immediate boost to Crown incomes. Annual revenue jumped from £29,315 to £82,797 in one year. However, the Book of Rates was not regularly revised. Gresham's use of Custom Farmers led to widespread corruption.

Church revenue: Elizabeth gained income from the First Fruits and Tenths tax on the clergy, profits from recusancy fines – which were increased significantly in 1581 – and by keeping bishoprics vacant for extended periods.

Parliamentary Taxation: grants came in two forms: a subsidy which raised around £100,000, and the fifteenths and tenths which raised around £30,000. Taxes in England were amongst the lowest in Europe.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs
heading: Inflation
summary: Inflation was a persistent problem throughout Elizabeth's reign, caused by population growth, poor harvests and Spanish bullion, which the government was unable to fully understand or address.
facts: Inflation had been a problem for every Tudor monarch. Although there had been a decline of inflation by the start of Elizabeth's reign, it accelerated in the 1560s. By the 1560s, average food prices were triple what they had been in the reign of Henry VII.

Population rise – between 1547 and 1603 the population of England increased from c.2.7 million to c.4 million. The availability of resources could not increase at the same rate. The increase in demand for resources therefore led to an increase of prices.
Poor harvests – made common by the Little Ice Age – decreased the supply of goods and thus increased prices.
Bullion – huge quantities of gold and silver arriving in Europe from the New World meant the value of these precious metals decreased. This meant coinage became less valuable and so prices rose.

Sir Thomas Gresham attempted to tackle inflation through recoinage in 1560. By 1561 the debased coins had been called in and the base alloys removed. However prices did not go down. Merchants simply set the same prices, or higher.
Elizabeth encouraged her people to limit demand by encouraging fasting during Lent and the observance of 'fish days' on Wednesdays and Fridays. The 1586 Book of Orders prohibited hoarding of grain.
Ultimately, the lack of understanding of how rising population's impact on supply and demand affected inflation meant the government could not tackle the issue.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs
heading: The cost of war
summary: The outbreak of war with Spain in 1585 destroyed Elizabeth's financial surplus, costing £4.5 million and forcing reliance on parliamentary taxation, monopolies and the sale of Crown lands.
facts: Even before the outbreak of war with Spain in 1585, the ongoing Dutch Revolt negatively affected English trade — a 1576 mutiny by Spanish troops in Antwerp destroyed much of that city, a centre for the English wool trade. Elizabeth's seizure of the Genoese Leon in 1568 prompted a trade embargo between England and Spain until 1573.

The Treaty of Nonsuch (1585) committed Elizabeth to £126,000 per year to support the Dutch rebels. In total the war cost Elizabeth £4.5 million — approximately £2 million in the Netherlands, £2 million in Ireland, £500,000 supporting Henry of Navarre and a further £160,000 to defend against the Spanish Armada.

The war did bring some benefits. Flemings fleeing the Netherlands in 1566 brought improved manufacturing skills to England. Francis Drake's circumnavigation (1577–80) and his 1587 raid on Cadiz (bringing £140,000) showed privateering could profit the Crown. The capture of the Madre de Dios in 1592 brought riches worth half the Crown's usual annual income.

However, Elizabeth's hard work at improving her finances was made redundant by the war. Her surplus of £300,000 was used almost entirely in the first year of war. Drake's 'English Armada' of 1589 against Spain was an unmitigated disaster. Attempts to intercept the treasure fleet from the New World routinely failed.

Due to the cost of war, Elizabeth was forced to resort to monopolies in her later years to reward her courtiers — these contributed to price rises and caused great dissatisfaction. Elizabeth was also forced to sell more Crown lands in the 1590s, further weakening long-term royal finances.

Parliament responded by granting unprecedented taxation — a double subsidy in 1589, and a triple subsidy in 1593 secured by Burghley. Five of Elizabeth's ten Parliaments were called after 1585, reflecting the increased need for parliamentary revenue. Despite tensions, the common enemy of Spain helped unite Parliament and Crown.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs
heading: Overseas trade
summary: Elizabeth sought to diversify English trade beyond the Antwerp cloth market through new trading companies, though the war with Spain severely disrupted commerce.
facts: Prior to Elizabeth's reign, English trade had been reliant on the export of wool to the cloth market in Antwerp. However, the Dutch Revolt and war with Spain led to the collapse of the Antwerp market as well as trade embargoes with Spain that severely hampered English trade.

Northern and Eastern Europe: the Muscovy Company was established in 1555 to trade English wool in Muscovy (Russia). In 1579 the Eastland Company was established with a depot in Poland to try to gain a foothold in trade in the Baltic.

The New World: Spain and Portugal dominated the New World. In 1562 Sir John Hawkins created the Triangular Slave Trade by capturing slaves in Sierra Leone and selling them for profit in the Caribbean.
The Middle East: in 1580 the Levant Company was founded to trade with the eastern shores of the Mediterranean, in particular the Ottoman Empire.
Asia: in 1600 the East India Company was founded which would trade with India.
Sir Walter Raleigh's attempts to create English colonies in North America on Roanoke Island failed.

Elizabeth herself was involved in the development of the Slave Trade. In 1596 the Privy Council gave permission for merchants to deport the hundreds of Black people living freely in England and sell them as slaves; despite slavery being illegal in England. In the end, this deportation never actually occurred.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs
heading: Causes of poverty and vagrancy
summary: Poverty and vagrancy grew throughout Elizabeth's reign due to population growth, enclosure and later the wars with Spain and Ireland, creating widespread social anxiety.
facts: Another consequence of the growing population (rising from 2.8 million in the 1540s to around 4.1 million by Elizabeth's death) was an increase in poverty and vagrancy. A surplus population led to increasing demand for work which allowed employers to lower wages. Simultaneously, landlords could raise rents.

Henry VIII's Dissolution of the Monasteries had removed a key source of charitable provision for the poor — monasteries had provided food, shelter and care for the destitute. This safety net was not replaced until the Poor Law legislation of Elizabeth's reign.

In the later years of Elizabeth's reign this was compounded by the wars with Spain and Ireland. Soldiers and sailors were discharged from service at arbitrary locations far from their homes, often with no pay and with serious injuries, adding to the numbers of destitute vagrants.

Contemporaries blamed poverty on greedy landlords and the practice of enclosure. By 1600, in some areas over 70% of available arable land had been enclosed — though enclosure was actually declining as the collapse of the Dutch cloth market reduced the incentive to convert to sheep farming.

Elizabethans were particularly afraid of vagrants. Ordinary people viewed vagrants as spreaders of disease and criminals. The government feared they would encourage social unrest — especially after the experience of 1549.

The death rate increased by 50% at the peak of the 1595–97 crisis, when a series of bad harvests combined with the socioeconomic pressures of war, taxation and population growth to create the most serious crisis of the reign.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs
heading: Government responses to poverty
summary: Government attitudes to poverty gradually shifted from punishment towards provision across Elizabeth's reign, culminating in the Poor Law of 1601.
facts: 1563 Statute of Artificers – attempt to increase long-term employment and prevent vagrancy. Introduced compulsory seven-year apprenticeships for craftspeople. JPs set maximum regional wages and discouraged economic migration in search of work. However, the Act proved impossible to enforce.
1563 Alms Act – the 'deserving poor' were to be supported by a Poor Rate organised by the Church. Contributions to the Poor Rate were not enforced by the state.

1572 Vagabonds Act – contributions to the Poor Rate made compulsory. Severe penalties enacted against vagrants and the 'undeserving/idle poor' including whipping, mutilation and, ultimately, execution.

1576 Act for the Relief of the Poor – 'Able-bodied' poor would be provided work, often in a House of Correction. First example of the state recognising the 'undeserving poor' also require help, not punishment.
1598 Act for the Relief of the Poor – begging was forbidden. JPs now appointed materials to employ the able-bodied poor.
1601 Poor Law – the government assumed the responsibility of providing for the Poor Rate from the Church. Provisions of the 1598 Acts became permanent. They would last until the mid-19th century.

Norwich, influenced by the experience of Kett's rebellion, banned begging. Instead the wealthiest citizens regularly contributed to a fund to support the poorest. Ipswich, Exeter and Cambridge all introduced similar schemes.

heading: Ireland and Tyrone's Rebellion
summary: Ireland was a persistent drain on Elizabeth's resources, culminating in Tyrone's Rebellion of 1594–1603 which cost £2 million to suppress and humiliated Essex.
facts: The English Crown had laid claim to Ireland since the 12th Century. However, by the 16th Century, English power was only truly felt in the Pale – the region around Dublin. Beyond the Pale, English authority was weak.

Throughout Elizabeth's reign, Ireland was a source of unrest which often spilled over into open revolt against the English Crown. The most notable include: the Fitzgerald Rebellions of 1569-73 and 1579-83; and Tyrone's Rebellion 1594-1603 also known as the Nine Years' War.

The most dangerous Irish rebellion was led by Hugh O'Neill, Earl of Tyrone. It came during the war with Spain which meant Elizabeth's resources were already stretched. Tyrone was able to gain national support across Ireland including from many powerful Irish earls. Tyrone won major victories against the English, most notably at Yellow Ford in 1598.

In 1599, the Earl of Essex led an English force of 16,000 – the largest force ever sent to Ireland – against Tyrone. He returned home against orders without fighting a battle. This humiliation led to his rebellion.

Essex's replacement – Lord Mountjoy – arrived in Ireland in 1600. He conciliated many of the Irish lords and by 1603 had forced Tyrone's surrender days after Elizabeth's death. Tyrone and the other Ulster lords fled to Europe – allowing Ulster to be colonised by Protestants.
In total it cost Elizabeth £2 million to defeat Tyrone's rebellion.

heading: Faction and Essex's rise
summary: Robert Devereux, Earl of Essex, became Elizabeth's favourite in the 1590s, his flamboyant personality and military successes masking his political recklessness and growing rivalry with the Cecils.
facts: Robert Devereux, the Earl of Essex, rose to Elizabeth's court as the godson of Leicester and due to his marriage to the daughter of Francis Walsingham. Essex's wit, eloquence and dashing personality quickly made him a favourite of the aging Elizabeth in the 1590s.
Essex was raised to the Privy Council in 1593, due to his personality more than his political skills.
On the Privy Council, Essex's flamboyant arrogance often clashed with the more pragmatic and capable Lord Burghley and his son, Robert Cecil.

Essex frequently acted unilaterally in the War with Spain: in 1589 Essex joined Drake's English Armada against Elizabeth's direct orders; in 1592 Essex disobeyed orders to confer with Henry IV of France without Elizabeth's permission; Essex's capture of Cadiz in 1596 made him extremely popular across England.

In the 1590s, following Leicester's death and due to Burghley's dotage, both Essex and Robert Cecil competed to be the principal figure on the Privy Council. In 1596, during Essex's expedition to Cadiz, Robert Cecil became Elizabeth's Secretary of State, thus securing control over the government.

The war exacerbated faction between the conservative, reactive councillors led by Burghley and Robert Cecil and the younger, more hawkish councillors led by Essex which created a lack of coherent policy.

heading: Essex's Rebellion
summary: Essex's disastrous Irish campaign and subsequent house arrest led to a desperate and poorly planned rebellion in 1601 that was quickly crushed.
facts: During discussions over how to deal with Tyrone's Rebellion, Essex reacted angrily to suggestions that Mountjoy should command — he expected the position himself. He was sent to Ireland with 16,000 men but never fought a battle, made an unauthorised truce with Tyrone and returned to London without permission.
Essex's defiant return enraged Elizabeth and Essex was placed under house arrest. His humiliation was compounded when Lord Mountjoy was sent to Ireland and succeeded where Essex had failed.

Whilst in house arrest, Essex lost his monopoly over sweet wines — his main source of income. He controversially commissioned a performance of Shakespeare's Richard II, which depicted the deposition of a weak and childless monarch. Elizabeth had banned the play. Essex commented 'I am Richard II, know ye not that?'

In desperation to reclaim his former position, Essex gathered a band of supporters in London including the Earl of Southampton. On 8 February 1601, he led them into the City of London hoping to raise popular rebellion against Cecil's dominance. Most of his supporters got cold feet — the rebellion was almost immediately defeated.

Essex and just five supporters were executed for treason in 1601. From then on, Robert Cecil's faction controlled government unopposed. Cecil managed the smooth transition of power to James VI of Scotland in 1603 — secretly corresponding with James throughout the final years of Elizabeth's reign.

heading: Socioeconomic unrest in the 1590s
summary: A series of bad harvests from 1594–1598 combined with the costs of war and taxation created serious social unrest in the 1590s, culminating in the Oxfordshire Rising of 1596.
facts: Despite efforts to manage the problem earlier in her reign, inflation persisted into the end of Elizabeth's reign. A series of bad harvests from 1594–98 led to the average price of wheat doubling. Cheaper grains like oats and rye increased in price at an even faster rate. At the peak of the crisis in 1595–97 the death rate increased by 50%.

Food shortages and poverty led to widespread unrest. Between 1595–98 there were food riots in Kent, Sussex, Somerset and Norfolk. Bands of roving unemployed men, many of them discharged soldiers, further threatened order.

The most notable example was the Oxfordshire Rising of 1596 — ostensibly a protest against enclosure, it came at the peak of the food crisis. The plot was discovered and the five ringleaders were publicly tried and executed as traitors. In the end only four people actually turned up — suggesting the threat of unrest was greater than the actual unrest.

During the war with Spain, Parliament approved unprecedented levels of taxation in 1589 and 1593. Tax collectors found it increasingly difficult to collect the full amount as the population was unable to pay. Elizabeth's granting of monopolies to her favourites often increased prices on staple goods.

Government action: the 1597 Tillage Act was passed to reverse any enclosure carried out since 1588. The 1598 Acts for the Relief of the Poor and Punishment of Rogues strengthened poor relief. The 1601 Poor Law formalised the system, making the state permanently responsible for the poor — provisions that lasted until the mid-19th century.

Local responses were often more innovative than central government — Norwich, influenced by the experience of Kett's rebellion, had banned begging and created a community fund. The contrast between effective local action and sluggish central response revealed the structural limits of Elizabethan government.

heading: Elizabeth's reputation
summary: Elizabeth carefully managed her public image through portraiture and pageantry, though in her final years scandal at court and socioeconomic problems undermined the myth of Gloriana.
facts: As with other monarchs, Elizabeth's power relied on her image. It was important that Elizabeth seemed strong and divinely ordained. Annual Accession Day Tilts on November 17 were lavishly celebrated to honour Elizabeth's virtues and portray her court as the apex of chivalry and loyalty.

As Elizabeth entered her 60s, her looks diminished. Her fondness for sugar had blackened her teeth; her grey hair was hidden by a bright red wig; her face, pockmarked from Smallpox in 1562, was always heavily made-up with white lead paint which was itself damaging to her skin.

In 1596 the Privy Council ordered the destruction of any 'unseemly and improper' portraits of Elizabeth — all had to be based on an agreed, flattering version produced by Nicholas Hilliard. In her official portraits Elizabeth still appeared as young as at her coronation in 1558.

Portraits like the Rainbow Portrait used heavy symbolism to enhance Elizabeth's image — she holds a rainbow (symbol of peace and divine favour); on her dress are eyes and ears (Elizabeth sees and hears all, no one can plot against her). Edmund Spenser's The Faerie Queene (1590) glorified Elizabeth as 'Gloriana'.

A series of scandals undermined Elizabeth's image at court. Walter Raleigh's disgrace for making Bess Throckmorton pregnant damaged the courtly image. Attendance at court tailed off and the nobility were sometimes reluctant to accompany Elizabeth on progress.

The socioeconomic unrest of the 1590s led to increased popular criticism — some commented 'We shall never have a merry world while the queen liveth'. Yet her final Parliament of 1601, with its famous Golden Speech on monopolies, was seen as a glorious final act — an old queen acknowledging her people's needs with characteristic grace.

unit: Chapter 1 – Origins of the Cold War to 1945
heading: Opposing ideologies
summary: The Cold War was rooted in the fundamental incompatibility of capitalism and communism as economic and political systems.
facts: Communism was constructed by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels in the 19th century. Marx argued capitalism would inevitably be overthrown by the workers (proletariat) in a socialist revolution, leading eventually to a classless, equal society.

Lenin developed Marx's ideas for Russia in the early 20th century, founding the Bolshevik Party in 1903, which seized power in October 1917. Under Lenin and then Stalin, the USSR became an authoritarian state with no democratic elections and limited freedom of speech.
Capitalism is an economic system based on private investment and profit. The West believed in the liberty of the individual, equality before the law, freedom of speech and elected government.
The USSR dismissed parliamentary democracy as a camouflage for capitalism. For Marxist-Leninists, democracy meant economic equality under the dictatorship of the proletariat.
Marxism-Leninism was opposed to religion — Marx called it 'the opium of the masses'. During the Russian Revolution, churches, mosques and synagogues were closed down and religion was banned.

In the West, Christian Churches were among the leading enemies of communism. In 1979 the election of Pope John Paul II of Poland as head of the Roman Catholic Church strengthened political opposition to communism in Poland.

unit: Chapter 1 – Origins of the Cold War to 1945
heading: Long-term tensions 1917–1941
summary: Deep mutual suspicion between the capitalist West and communist USSR pre-dated the Cold War by over two decades.
facts: The Bolshevik Revolution of October 1917 alarmed Western powers — Britain, the USA, France and Japan had all intervened in Russia's Civil War (1917–22) on the side of the Whites against the communist Reds.
The establishment of the Comintern in 1919 — an international organisation to promote communism — confirmed Western fears that the USSR sought to export revolution.

The 1920s and 1930s saw a 'Red Scare' in the USA as fear of communist infiltration grew. The USSR's nationalisation of the economy led to loss of foreign investment and Soviet refusal to honour debts owed by previous Russian governments.

Stalin's show trials and oppression in the 1930s reinforced Western perceptions of the USSR as a brutal dictatorship. The 1938 Munich Agreement (Western appeasement of Hitler) convinced Stalin that the West wanted Germany and Russia to fight each other.
The Nazi-Soviet Pact of August 1939 shocked the West — it seemed to confirm that communism and fascism had more in common than communism and democracy.

Operation Barbarossa in June 1941 transformed relations — Churchill was quick to see the potential of Soviet might and forged the Grand Alliance. The USSR's image was transformed in the West from a brutal dictatorship to patriots bravely resisting the Nazis, led by 'Uncle Joe' Stalin.

unit: Chapter 1 – Origins of the Cold War to 1945
heading: Wartime tensions in the Grand Alliance
summary: Despite their alliance against Hitler, the USA, USSR and Britain were divided by the second front, Poland and their competing visions for post-war Europe.
facts: The Atlantic Charter (August 1941) was a joint British and American document affirming war aims including self-determination and political freedom. Although the USSR 'endorsed' it, it was not part of writing it and it represented a severe threat to Soviet ideas.

The USSR proposed that the Allies create a Second Front through France. Stalin felt he had been fighting the bulk of the war in Europe alone while the Western Allies defended their territories in North Africa. Britain and the USA stalled on opening the Second Front until June 1944, causing Stalin to doubt their commitment to Soviet security.

Poland proved deeply divisive. The West wanted a free and democratic Poland as they had gone to war to uphold Polish independence. The USSR saw Poland as a vital buffer zone and had seized territory from it as part of the Nazi-Soviet Pact. Britain was hosting the Polish government in exile, hoping to restore them at the end of the war.

In October 1944, Churchill visited Moscow and brokered the 'Percentages Agreement' — dividing Eastern Europe into spheres of influence between Russia and the West. This showed the contempt both leaders had for the wishes of Eastern Europeans. The USA would not have agreed.
By 1945, Roosevelt had accepted Russian domination of Eastern Europe and Churchill had realised that Britain could no longer exert major influence on world affairs.

The changes in leadership at Potsdam — Truman replacing Roosevelt and Attlee replacing Churchill — meant the strong personal relations of the 'Big Three' could no longer guide international affairs. Truman had much less inclination to make concessions to Stalin.

unit: Chapter 1 – Origins of the Cold War to 1945
heading: The Tehran and Yalta Conferences
summary: Tehran and Yalta produced agreements on the post-war world but left key questions — especially over Poland and Eastern Europe — unresolved.
facts: Tehran, November 1943: the 'Big Three' met for the first time. Main aims were to direct wartime strategy — the USA and UK promised to open a second front. There was a vague idea that Germany would remain weak after the war.
Yalta, February 1945 (Roosevelt, Stalin, Churchill): by Yalta it was clear the Nazis would lose the war — attention shifted to the post-war world.

Agreed at Yalta: Germany would be split into four zones of occupation; Berlin, inside the Soviet zone, would also be divided into four zones; Germany would pay $20 billion in reparations, half to the USSR; a United Nations organisation would be established.
Agreed at Yalta: Stalin promised that Eastern Europe would have free elections. Eastern Europe would be a Soviet 'sphere of influence' — though this was never clearly defined.

Disagreed at Yalta: Poland. Stalin wanted a 'friendly' Polish government (the Lublin Committee). Britain had hosted the Polish government in exile and had gone to war to defend Poland's independence. There was little to guarantee Stalin would actually allow free elections.
Stalin wanted greater representation for individual Soviet republics in the UN, fearing it would become anti-Soviet. Roosevelt saw the UN as the hope for the future.
