heading: The Potsdam Conference
summary: Potsdam revealed a dramatic escalation of tension — the common enemy was defeated, Roosevelt was dead, and the atomic bomb had been used without telling Stalin.
facts: Potsdam, July–August 1945 (Truman, Stalin, Attlee): Hitler's death in May had removed the common enemy. Roosevelt's death in April had brought in Truman, who was far more hostile to Stalin. Churchill lost the British election mid-conference and was replaced by Attlee.
Between Yalta and Potsdam, Stalin had installed a communist puppet government in Poland, breaking his promise of free elections. This confirmed Truman's worst suspicions about Soviet intentions.
Agreed at Potsdam: Germany to be divided into four zones as agreed at Yalta; reparations to be taken from each occupying zone; Nazi war criminals to be tried at Nuremberg.

Disagreed at Potsdam: Britain and America did not want to implement harsh reparations on Germany — they feared a repeat of Versailles and wanted Germany to recover as a buffer against communism. Stalin, who had lost 25 million people in the war, wanted very harsh reparations.

During the conference the Americans dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima (6th August) and Nagasaki (9th August). Truman had informed Stalin only vaguely. Stalin saw this as a direct threat — the USSR could not compete with nuclear weapons.
The conference ended with very few new agreements but a great deal of tension. No general peace settlement ended the war — Truman and Stalin were poised for the confrontations of the Cold War.

heading: Liberation of Europe — East vs West
summary: The different ways East and West liberated Europe from Nazi rule created fundamentally different political realities that deepened Cold War division.
facts: Allied Control Commissions (ACCs) were set up in each occupied territory. The precedent was that the country which had done the bulk of the 'liberating' had more sway on the ACC — so the USSR dominated ACCs in Romania, Bulgaria, Finland and Hungary.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955
heading: The creation of the United Nations
summary: The UN was created in 1945 as an international peacekeeping organisation, but immediately became a battleground for Cold War tensions.
facts: The United Nations was established on 24 October 1945, replacing the ineffective League of Nations which had failed to prevent WWII. Its headquarters were in Manhattan, New York City, reflecting the rise of the United States to global leadership.

The Security Council was the UN's most powerful body — the five permanent members (USA, USSR, UK, France and China) each had the power of veto. This immediately gave the USSR the ability to block any measure it disagreed with.

At its first meeting in 1946, the Security Council immediately became a Cold War arena. Iran raised the matter of Russian-occupied Azerbaijan; Russia countered by opening the issue of British troops in Greece. Russia used the first Security Council veto to block a plan for Britain and France to withdraw from Syria and Lebanon.

The Atomic Control Commission was created at the first UN meeting to 'deal with problems raised by the discovery of atomic energy'. The USA proposed international control of atomic weapons; the USSR rejected this as they did not yet have their own bomb and feared American dominance.

Stalin had insisted on greater representation for individual Soviet republics in the UN, fearing it would become anti-Soviet. He eventually won representation for Ukraine and Byelorussia as separate members alongside the USSR.

Despite the Cold War tensions, the UN provided a forum for diplomacy and debate that helped prevent direct superpower conflict. It played a role in the Korean War (1950–53) when the USSR was boycotting the Security Council and the USA was able to pass a resolution authorising military action.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955
heading: The Iron Curtain speech and its significance
summary: Churchill's Iron Curtain speech of March 1946 gave voice to Western fears about Soviet expansionism and helped harden attitudes on both sides.
facts: In March 1946, Churchill made a speech in Fulton, Missouri, calling it 'The Sinews of Peace'. He coined the famous phrase: 'From Stettin in the Baltic to Trieste in the Adriatic, an iron curtain has descended across the continent.'

Key ideas in the speech: Europe was firmly divided; the USSR controlled all Eastern European countries equally; the West needed to negotiate from a position of strength; the USSR wanted to expand without limit and to export communism.
Churchill's key ideas: Stalin was admiring of strength and despising of weakness — the West must deal with him 'supported by the whole strength of the English-speaking world'.

Reactions: Stalin reacted by accusing Churchill of being 'a firebrand of war' and arguing the USSR had only peaceful ambitions. Many in the USA thought the speech was irresponsible. Truman did not immediately signify his approval.

The speech's accuracy was flawed — Soviet influence was not yet uniform across Eastern Europe. Berlin was not under total Soviet control; total Soviet domination was not yet established in Prague; Yugoslavia under Tito was resisting Moscow.

Despite its inaccuracies, the vivid image of the speech helped to encourage anti-Russian sentiment and provoked equally strong rhetoric from the USSR, ramping up tension and verbal conflict. By 1946 the mood in the USA was shifting away from isolationism to opposing communist expansion.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955
heading: Soviet control of Eastern Europe — salami tactics
summary: Between 1945 and 1948, the USSR used salami tactics to install communist governments across Eastern Europe, turning it into a Soviet buffer zone.
facts: The USSR's method of taking control became known as 'salami tactics' — entering into coalition governments with other parties, then when the time was right 'slicing them out' of coalition governments. Elections were carefully controlled by violence and intimidation. There was extensive propaganda and the establishment of political police.

Poland: Soviet forces set up a Provisional Government in June 1945 dominated by Polish communists. When the London Poles (government in exile) joined, it was obvious there would be no free elections. By 1947 the communist-dominated government had repressed all opposition.

Romania: a new government was imposed on the king by the USSR in December 1945. By violence and pressure, the communist-dominated National Democratic Front won 80% of the vote in November 1946. In December 1947 the king was forced to abdicate.

Hungary: Stalin allowed free elections in November 1945. By 1947 the leading opposition leader was arrested. In March 1948 socialists were forced to merge with communists — the Independent Front became the only party.

Czechoslovakia: elections in March 1946 gave Czech communists 38% of the vote and were genuinely free. However the USSR was determined to prevent the Czechs accepting Marshall Aid. In February 1948 a communist coup took place. Foreign minister Jan Masaryk was thrown from a window, probably by the security police. President Benes was forced to resign.

By 1948, unrepresentative pro-Moscow communist leaders had been established and opposition was destroyed by arrests, intimidation and murder. The Long Telegram (February 1946) from US ambassador Kennan confirmed Truman's fears — Stalin was planning the destruction of capitalism and world communism. The Novikov Telegram (September 1946) told Stalin that the US were planning to use their new military might to dominate the world.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955
heading: The Truman Doctrine and Marshall Aid
summary: The Truman Doctrine and Marshall Plan committed the USA to actively containing communism and rebuilding Western Europe economically.
facts: On 12 March 1947, Truman appealed to Congress to strengthen non-communist forces in areas thought vulnerable to communist domination. He set out two competing ways of life: one based on free institutions, representative government and individual freedom; the other based on terror, oppression and the will of a minority imposed on a majority.

It was the policy of the USA to support free peoples who resist subjugation by armed minorities or outside pressures. The USA was committed to an active foreign policy of containment — using its economic and military power to intervene in European and world affairs.

The trigger: Britain's inability to keep financing anti-communist fighters in Greece in 1947 made it clear the US needed to accept responsibility to halt communism's spread. By 1947 Stalin was not keeping to his agreements at Yalta about elections in Eastern Europe. Large communist parties existed in Italy and France.

The follow-up was the Marshall Plan of June 1947 — Secretary of State George Marshall offered an aid package of $13 billion to Europe. No distinction was made between 'free' and 'unfree' countries, but Stalin forbade Soviet-dominated nations to attend the Paris meeting to discuss it — 16 nations attended without them.
Stalin was furious — he labelled the plan 'Dollar Imperialism', arguing America was creating an economic empire in Europe. He feared it would pull Eastern European states out of the Soviet orbit.

Results: Most of the $12.7 billion in aid was used to purchase goods and raw materials from the USA. It supported the re-industrialisation of West Germany, promoting political stability after 1949. It strengthened anti-communist feeling in the USA and hostility in the Communist bloc.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955
heading: Cominform and Comecon
summary: The USSR's response to the Truman Doctrine and Marshall Plan was to create two organisations to tighten its ideological and economic control over Eastern Europe.
facts: Stalin banned Soviet bloc governments from accepting Marshall Aid and called a conference of all European communist parties in Poland. From this, the Communist Information Bureau (Cominform) emerged in September 1947.

Cominform was intended as propaganda to prevent any communist party being lured by US 'dollar diplomacy'. Its aims were to 'provide information to strengthen the anti-imperialist democratic camp, the principal aim of which is to undermine imperialism, strengthen democracy and liquidate the remnants of fascism'.

The most enthusiastic party was the Yugoslav — its first headquarters was in Belgrade. However, after the rift between Tito and Stalin in 1948 and Yugoslavia's expulsion from Cominform, it moved to Bucharest. It was abolished in 1956.

Tito resisted Stalin's control — he wanted to apply for Marshall Aid and refused to subordinate Yugoslavia to Moscow. When Moscow sent letters of complaint, the Yugoslavian Communist Party pointed out they had not been liberated by the Soviet Union. Tito-ists (communists who believed national parties should be independent of the USSR) were expelled from communist parties across Eastern Europe.

The Council of Mutual Economic Assistance (Comecon) was formed in 1949 as an economic alliance parallel to the Marshall Plan. Initial members were the USSR, Albania, Bulgaria, Romania, Hungary, Poland and Czechoslovakia.

Comecon helped divide Europe into two competing economic blocs. It boosted the USSR's control of its satellites — economic life was dominated by relations between Comecon members and the USSR, providing an outlet for Soviet manufacturers and a supply of raw materials. After 1956 more ambitious regional policies were attempted.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955
heading: Conflicts over Germany and the Berlin Blockade
summary: Germany became the central battleground of the early Cold War, culminating in the Berlin Blockade of 1948–49 — the most dangerous confrontation yet.
facts: Germany was divided into four occupation zones (American, British, French and Soviet) agreed at Yalta and Potsdam. Berlin, inside the Soviet zone, was also divided into four sectors. The two sides had very different views about how to treat Germany — the USSR wanted reparations and a weak Germany; the West wanted Germany to recover as a buffer against communism.

In January 1947 Bizonia was created from the US and British zones. In June 1948, the West introduced a new currency — the Deutschmark — for West Germany without consulting the USSR. The USSR created its own currency for the East, the Ostmark.
Stalin's key aim was to prevent the creation of a West German state. He chose to put pressure on the West's weakest point — West Berlin, an island of Western democracy deep inside the Soviet zone.

On 23 June 1948 Stalin imposed a blockade on all road and rail links to West Berlin and cut off its electricity. The Allies supplied the city by air — each day 2,000 tonnes of supplies were flown in. As a threat, 60 B29 bombers were stationed in eastern England. The airlift was extended, reaching 8,000 tonnes a day by February 1949.

The blockade and airlift ended in May 1949. Stalin could not afford to allow Germany to exercise political freedom and the damage done to the USSR in the German invasion of 1941 seemed to justify reparations. But the West was willing to risk confrontation with the USSR to prevent Soviet expansion westwards.
The blockade was a propaganda disaster for the USSR — it confirmed the view of the Soviet Union as an aggressor. It accelerated the formation of NATO and the creation of two separate German states.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955
heading: The creation of East and West Germany
summary: The Berlin Blockade accelerated the permanent division of Germany into two separate states with opposing political and economic systems.
facts: When France agreed to join Bizonia (creating Trizonia) in April 1949, it was clear separate states would emerge. The West approved the Basic Law — the constitution for West Germany — in spring 1949. Elections took place in August and Konrad Adenauer became Chancellor.

West Germany (the Federal Republic) became one of the most closely controlled, economically and politically, of all the satellite states. By the 1950s it had experienced an 'economic miracle' — a developed capitalist consumer economy with trade links to the Common Market and US aid. Its leadership was unhesitatingly supportive of Washington.

In East Germany, the dominant party was the SED — a coalition of former socialists and communists, in practice dominated by pro-Moscow Marxists. In May 1949 the People's Council approved a constitution. The German Democratic Republic (DDR) was officially created in October 1949.

East Germany and East Berlin remained impoverished and drab — an old-fashioned economy based on restrictive controls and wasteful production. Stalin remained uncommitted to an independent East Germany and was prepared to sacrifice it as late as 1952, when he offered reunification in return for a neutral Germany.

Fear and dislike of the SED led to the establishment of a West Berlin city government. Officially the four-power Control Commission ran the city, but West Berlin sent representatives to the Bonn parliament. East Berlin became the capital of the DDR.

West Germany and West Berlin represented the great success story of the Allies — the Nazi past was put aside, there was an economic miracle and stable, conservative politics. It became a model of capitalist development.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955
heading: The East German Rising 1953
summary: The East German Rising of June 1953 was the first major challenge to Soviet control in Eastern Europe — suppressed by Soviet tanks and revealing the fragility of the DDR.
facts: By 1953 the DDR was in serious difficulty. The Stalinist leader Walter Ulbricht had imposed harsh economic policies — collectivisation, high production quotas and low wages. The standard of living was far below that of West Germany and the 'brain drain' through Berlin was accelerating.

In June 1953, following Stalin's death in March, the Soviet leadership initially encouraged Ulbricht to adopt a 'New Course' — relaxing some of the harsher economic policies. However, Ulbricht refused to reduce the increased work quotas he had just imposed on factory workers.

On 16–17 June 1953, workers in East Berlin went on strike and took to the streets, initially demanding the withdrawal of the increased work quotas. The protests rapidly spread across the DDR to over 400 towns and cities — around 400,000 people participated. Demands quickly became political: free elections and the end of the SED regime.
Soviet tanks were deployed on 17 June to suppress the uprising. Around 55 people were killed, 20 were executed and thousands were arrested. The uprising was crushed within days.

Significance: the East German Rising showed how shallow the roots of communism were in the DDR — workers were rising against a workers' state. The USSR's willingness to use tanks showed it would not allow regime change in its satellite states.

In the West, 17 June became a national holiday in West Germany — 'Tag der Deutschen Einheit' (Day of German Unity) — until reunification in 1990. Khrushchev subsequently supported Ulbricht's suggestion of greater controls on the Berlin border, leading eventually to the Berlin Wall.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955
heading: NATO and the Warsaw Pact
summary: The failure to agree a European peace settlement led to the creation of two rival military alliances that hardened the division of Europe into armed camps.
facts: In March 1947 France and Britain signed the Treaty of Dunkirk. By 1948, fears about Soviet aggression (especially the communist coup in Czechoslovakia) led to the Brussels Pact — binding Belgium, Britain, France, Luxemburg and the Netherlands into a mutual defence pact against the USSR.

Secret talks between Britain, Canada and the USA led to the North Atlantic Treaty of 4 April 1949 — NATO. It promised consultation on issues of mutual interest and assistance in the event of an attack on any one member country. It also had an ideological element — defending not merely national security but 'freedom, common heritage and civilisation'.

NATO expansion: in September 1949 it was learnt that Stalin had atomic weapons. In 1950, communist North Korea invaded non-communist South Korea. NATO countries joined the Korean War 1950–53 to expel the North Korean invaders. In 1952 the Lisbon Conference set up a permanent HQ in Paris with a permanent military force of 35 divisions.

The Warsaw Pact was signed on 14 May 1955 by the USSR and most of its Eastern European satellites (the DDR signed in 1956). Unlike NATO, it was not an agreement between independent states — it was a policy move by the USSR in response to West Germany joining NATO.

The Warsaw Pact promised consultation on mutual interest and assistance in the event of attack on any one member. If 'a general European treaty of Collective Security' were signed — i.e. reunification of a neutral Germany — it would lapse, indicating it was more a political than a defensive move.

Though it seemed to divide Europe into armed camps, little had changed — Moscow already controlled the foreign and defence policies of its Eastern European allies. But it did mean suppression of discontent would now be by 'the Warsaw Pact' rather than the USSR alone — a convenient fiction.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955
heading: The Arms Race
summary: Both superpowers developed increasingly destructive nuclear arsenals, creating a world where war would mean mutually assured destruction.
facts: The USA dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki on 6th and 9th August 1945, ending WWII with Japan. This was a huge threat to the USSR — they could not compete with nuclear weapons. Stalin immediately accelerated the Soviet nuclear weapons programme.

The USSR successfully tested its first atomic bomb in 1949 — years earlier than the West had expected. This shocked the West and led to the growth of NATO. In 1952 the USA tested the first hydrogen bomb — vastly more destructive than the atomic bomb. The USSR tested its own hydrogen bomb in 1953.

From the mid-1950s, the development of missiles led to a second and more deadly arms race. In August 1957 the USSR tested a successful ICBM (intercontinental ballistic missile). The launch of the Sputnik satellite showed that Soviet technology was no longer lagging behind.

The USA shifted its strategic policy to 'mutually assured destruction' (MAD) — the assumption that Russian attacks would lead to devastating retaliatory strikes with the capacity to destroy half the Russian population and 80% of its industry.

The USSR developed MIRVs (multiple independently targeted re-entry vehicles) from 1964 — warheads that could target US missile silos with extreme precision. The USA developed its own MIRVs and also Polaris submarines equipped with missiles.

Pressure to end the race came from peace movements in the West and from summits — but the mutual suspicion on both sides prevented these from being very effective.

subheadings.label: The nuclear arms race
facts: The USA dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki on 6th and 9th August 1945, ending WWII with Japan. This was a huge threat to the USSR — they could not compete with nuclear weapons. Stalin immediately accelerated the Soviet nuclear weapons programme.

heading: De-Stalinisation and the Polish Crisis
summary: Khrushchev's denunciation of Stalin in 1956 raised hopes across Eastern Europe for reform, triggering the Polish October that showed the limits of Soviet flexibility.
facts: Stalin's death in March 1953 encouraged hopes for change in Eastern Europe. Communism had shallow roots in largely agrarian societies, and the imposition of Soviet economic policies — collectivisation, forced industrialisation and state controls — had caused deep resentment.

In February 1956 Khrushchev gave his 'secret speech' at the 20th Party Congress denouncing Stalin's crimes — the purges, show trials, cult of personality and abuse of power. This 'de-Stalinisation' raised hopes of liberalisation across Eastern Europe.

In Poland, protests began in June 1956 at the Poznan factories — initially demanding better wages but quickly becoming political. The party itself was divided — the more liberal wing asserted itself and refused to accept Russia's nominee as defence minister.

Khrushchev accepted Gomulka rather than launching a massive invasion. Gomulka proved to be a limited reformer — loyal to the USSR and to the Warsaw Pact. The unrest in Poland was a major factor in similar unrest in Hungary.

De-Stalinisation showed the limits of Soviet control — Khrushchev had to accept that some reform was necessary to maintain stability. But it also showed the limits of reform — Gomulka only went so far before Moscow's tolerance ran out.

heading: The Hungarian Uprising 1956
summary: The Hungarian Uprising of October–November 1956 was the most serious challenge to Soviet control of Eastern Europe — brutally crushed and revealing the limits of Western containment.
facts: Hungary resented Stalinist policies and the domination of Stalinist leader Rakosi — who was heavily dependent on repression. The condemnation of Stalinism weakened the leadership. Political rallies spread and on 23 October 1956 the police fired on protesters, leading to workers joining students and intellectuals.

Imre Nagy — a previously disgraced liberal communist — took power. He began to implement reforms: ended the one-party state by introducing non-communists into government, authorised release of political prisoners and asked Khrushchev to remove Soviet troops from Hungary. Khrushchev accepted in the hope of ending the protests.
However Nagy went too far — he announced Hungary would leave the Warsaw Pact and become a neutral non-aligned country. This could cause a chain reaction across the Eastern bloc.

Khrushchev ordered the invasion of Hungary. The sheer size of the military force — over a thousand tanks deployed — made resistance impossible. Janos Kadar was appointed leader and — after seeming to be liberal — imposed Moscow's rule brutally. Nagy was executed and some 180,000 Hungarians fled to the West.

The Hungarians had hoped for Western help but none came — the USA disapproved but did not intervene. The attention of the world was diverted by the British and French invasion of Suez in 1956. This showed that America would not interfere to defend the satellite states.

Consequences: the failure of the USA to intervene revealed the limitations of containment. There was little long-term interruption of contacts between East and West — NATO was a defensive alliance and the West had already accepted Hungary as part of the Soviet bloc.

heading: West German rearmament and NATO entry
summary: West Germany's rearmament and entry into NATO in 1955 alarmed the USSR, confirming Soviet fears and directly triggering the creation of the Warsaw Pact.
facts: The question of West German rearmament was highly controversial. Many — particularly in France — feared a rearmed Germany would again threaten European peace. However, the Korean War (1950–53) showed that NATO needed more ground forces in Europe.
A European Defence Community (EDC) was proposed in 1950 — a European army with German units. France, however, rejected the EDC in August 1954, fearing German dominance of a European force.

A compromise was reached: in October 1954 France was persuaded to agree to a limited West German army. Germany was not to have nuclear weapons and British forces would remain in Germany as a safeguard. West Germany joined NATO in May 1955.

The East German leadership under Ulbricht had been building up a paramilitary police force of 60,000. West German rearmament strengthened the division of Germany and also contributed to the creation of the Warsaw Pact (May 1955) — signed just days after West Germany joined NATO.

The USSR responded by offering to support German reunification and the creation of a neutral Germany that would not join either the EDC or NATO — little came of this, and Ulbricht was allowed to begin a more doctrinaire socialist policy in the DDR.

West German rearmament increased the flow of East Germans fleeing to the West — they feared a rearmed Germany would eventually try to reclaim lost territory. By 1961, 3.5 million East Germans had left — 20% of the population — creating the crisis that led to the Berlin Wall.

heading: The Berlin Wall
summary: The Berlin Wall of August 1961 halted the brain drain from East Germany — a propaganda disaster that confirmed communism's failure.
facts: Khrushchev needed to show the world — and the critical Chinese communists — that Soviet economic policies worked. Yet in East Germany they were obviously failing. The 'brain drain' could not continue.

Summit meetings 1959–61 failed to resolve the issue. The Paris summit (1960) collapsed when a US U-2 spy plane was shot down over the USSR.

Ulbricht and his colleagues may have taken the decision on 12 August 1961. The frontier was closed that night and barriers erected, leading to the building of a wall on 17 August. A second, inner wall was constructed in 1962 with a 'zone of death' between. Some 5,000 managed to escape up to 1989 and there were possibly 136 deaths among those attempting to escape.

heading: The Cuban Missile Crisis
summary: The Cuban Missile Crisis of October 1962 brought the superpowers closer to nuclear war than at any other point — resolved through secret diplomacy and mutual compromise.
facts: Cuba had been a US ally until Fidel Castro's communist revolution in 1959. The USA sponsored the failed Bay of Pigs invasion in 1961 — an attempt to overthrow Castro by CIA-trained Cuban exiles. Khrushchev placed nuclear missiles in Cuba to defend it and to counter US Jupiter missiles in Turkey which were a direct threat to the USSR.

In October 1962 a U-2 spy plane photographed Soviet missile installations in Cuba. Kennedy was presented with two options: an air strike to destroy the missiles, or a naval blockade ('quarantine'). Kennedy chose the blockade and demanded the missiles be removed.

For 13 days the world held its breath as Soviet ships carrying missiles approached the US quarantine line. Soviet submarines were in the area. Kennedy and Khrushchev exchanged letters — Khrushchev eventually offered to remove the missiles if the USA pledged not to invade Cuba.

A second letter from Khrushchev added a demand that US Jupiter missiles be removed from Turkey. Kennedy publicly accepted the pledge not to invade Cuba and secretly agreed to remove the Turkish missiles.

Consequences for Khrushchev: America had been forced to remove its Jupiter missiles from Turkey; Cuba remained communist and America would not invade. However Khrushchev was seen to have backed down first and was ousted in 1964, replaced by Brezhnev.

Consequences for Kennedy: seen to have 'won' — Khrushchev backed down and the Cuban missiles were removed. Kennedy was seen as strong and having stood up to Khrushchev. Consequences for both: 1963 — nuclear 'hotline' established. 1963 — Limited Test Ban Treaty. 1968 — Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty. The crisis made both sides more determined to avoid future nuclear confrontations.

heading: The Space Race
summary: The Space Race became a key arena of Cold War competition — a battle for technological prestige that the USSR initially led but the USA ultimately won.
facts: The Space Race grew out of the arms race — missile technology underpinned both. The early 1950s saw considerable US interest in space and science fiction, which reflected fears of communism and the infiltration of an 'alien' ideology into US life.

Sputnik, October 1957: despite a lot of US research, it was the USSR that made the first major advance into space — launching the first man-made satellite. Sputnik circled the Earth once every 90 minutes at a speed of 28,000 miles an hour. This shocked the USA — it showed Soviet technology was no longer lagging behind and that a Russian satellite crossing the USA could theoretically be weaponised.

The USSR continued to lead: in November 1957 they put a dog (Laika) into space. On 12 April 1961 Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space aboard Vostok 1. The first woman in space was Valentina Tereshkova (June 1963) and the first spacewalk was by Alexei Leonov (March 1965).

US response: the USA formed NASA using the rocket knowledge of German scientist Werner von Braun. In February 1962 John Glenn made a successful voyage in space. Kennedy made the challenge explicit in September 1962, pledging to put a man on the moon by the end of the decade.

US achievement: Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed on the moon on 20 July 1969. The considerable resources taken by this Race and the efforts to control the parallel arms race by the SALT led to greater cooperation.

The first joint US–Soviet space mission — the Apollo-Soyuz Mission — took place in 1975, symbolising the spirit of détente. The Space Race led to considerable excitement about the possibilities of space travel, heroism and technological advances.

heading: The Czech Crisis 1968
summary: The Prague Spring of 1968 threatened Soviet control of Eastern Europe — crushed by invasion and triggering the Brezhnev Doctrine.
facts: Czechoslovakia had been a prosperous democracy before WWII. Under Soviet rule, discontent was high — the economy was run for the good of the USSR rather than Czechoslovakia; there was no freedom of speech; there were purges between 1949 and 1954. By the 1960s the Czech economy was in serious decline.

In January 1968, Alexander Dubček became leader of the Czech Communist Party and launched the 'Prague Spring' — a programme of liberalisation including freedom of speech, freedom of the press, freedom of movement and multi-party democracy. He called it 'socialism with a human face'.

The USSR was alarmed — if the Czechs could liberalise, other satellite states would follow. Brezhnev warned Dubček repeatedly but Dubček refused to abandon his reforms. The Czechs argued they had the right to determine their own path to socialism.

In August 1968 the USSR, Poland, Hungary, Bulgaria and East Germany invaded Czechoslovakia with 500,000 troops. Dubček was captured by Soviet paratroopers, taken to Moscow and 'encouraged' to abandon his reforms. 150 Czechoslovak civilians were killed in resistance. Jan Palach set himself on fire in protest. Hard-line Gustáv Husák replaced Dubček.

Consequences: America failed to help — too distracted by Vietnam. Albania left the Warsaw Pact in protest. Yugoslavia and Romania condemned the invasion and began to foster closer links with China. Western communist parties cut ties with the USSR in protest. The invasion weakened Soviet control of Eastern Europe in the long run.

heading: The Brezhnev Doctrine
summary: The Brezhnev Doctrine asserted the USSR's right to intervene in any communist country showing signs of turning towards capitalism — the ideological justification for Soviet imperialism.
facts: Following the invasion of Czechoslovakia in August 1968, Brezhnev issued his doctrine to justify the intervention: if any communist country was showing signs of turning towards capitalism, it was the responsibility of all communist countries to force it back to communism.

The doctrine asserted the concept of 'limited sovereignty' — communist states were not fully sovereign if their actions threatened the socialist bloc as a whole. This directly contradicted the UN Charter's principle of national self-determination.

In practice, the Brezhnev Doctrine meant that any satellite state attempting to leave the Warsaw Pact or adopt a multi-party system would face Soviet military intervention — as Hungary had in 1956 and Czechoslovakia in 1968.
The Doctrine cast a long shadow over Eastern Europe. It made clear to reformers in Poland, Hungary and Czechoslovakia that there were firm limits to how far they could challenge Soviet authority.

Western communist parties were appalled — many cut ties with the USSR in protest at the invasion of Czechoslovakia. This process, known as 'Eurocommunism', saw Western communist parties increasingly distance themselves from Moscow.

Gorbachev replaced the Brezhnev Doctrine with the 'Sinatra Doctrine' in 1988 — satellite states were now free to 'do it their way'. This was the single most important decision enabling the 1989 revolutions, as it removed the threat of Soviet military intervention.

heading: Solidarity in Poland 1980–81
summary: The Solidarity movement in Poland was the most serious challenge to Soviet-bloc communist authority since Hungary in 1956 — contained by martial law rather than Soviet invasion.
facts: Economic unrest — including strikes in the Gdansk shipyards in 1980 — led the Polish government to recognise the Solidarity trade union movement. Solidarity, led by Lech Walesa, was the first independent trade union in the Eastern bloc.

In April 1981 the Round Table Agreements saw Solidarity recognised as a political party. There was to be a new constitution, with Solidarity allowed to compete with the Communist Party for 35% of the seats in a lower house of parliament. There would be free elections for the second chamber.

However the USSR viewed Solidarity with deep alarm. A non-communist government in Poland would be unacceptable. Brezhnev threatened intervention. The Polish Communist Party leader Jaruzelski declared martial law in December 1981, suspending Solidarity and arresting its leaders including Walesa.

The elections of June 1981 resulted in a Solidarity government with some Communists holding major posts. The existing leader, Jaruzelski, remained president and Communists held key posts in the new government.

Poland remained part of the Warsaw Pact but the USSR had accepted a non-Communist government and important constitutional change. This was a landmark — the first time the USSR had allowed a satellite state to move significantly away from communist one-party rule.

The role of Pope John Paul II — a Pole elected in 1979 — was crucial. His visits to Poland strengthened the resolve of the Polish people. The Catholic Church provided an alternative source of authority and community to the communist state.

heading: Détente and SALT
summary: Détente — the period of improved relations from 1969 to 1979 — produced landmark arms limitation agreements but ultimately failed to resolve the fundamental tensions of the Cold War.
facts: Détente is the term used for the period of improved relations between the USA and USSR from 1969 to 1980. Its roots lay in the Cuban Missile Crisis — both sides had come so close to nuclear war that they recognised the need for greater communication and arms control.

Reasons for détente: the USSR faced worsening relations with China — there were serious border clashes in 1969 and the USSR secretly asked the USA's reaction to a joint action against China's nuclear installations. The USA faced the costly Vietnam War and the sudden rise in oil prices in 1973. Both sides recognised that arms reduction would help their economies.

SALT I (1972): the Strategic Arms Limitation Talks established a 5-year freeze on constructing missile launchers and a freeze on ICBMs and submarine-launched ballistic missiles. Both sides agreed to restrict anti-ballistic screens to their capital cities and main missile sites. Nixon and Brezhnev visited each other in 1972/3.

Helsinki Accords (1975): 33 nations from NATO and the Warsaw Pact met. Three 'baskets' were agreed: Basket 1 — European borders are inviolable; Basket 2 — economic and scientific co-operation; Basket 3 — human rights are to be respected. Later that year, the Apollo-Soyuz Mission followed up the spirit of Basket 2.

SALT II (1979): proposed new treaty with greater bans on strategic bombers and ICBMs. Talks stalled and were eventually cancelled by President Carter due to growing distrust of the Soviet government, the Iranian Revolution of 1979, and the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan.

In practice détente was 'just a piece of paper' — both sides still had enough nuclear weapons to initiate MAD. The human rights provisions of Helsinki were regularly ignored by the USSR. But it symbolised improving relations and reduced the immediate risk of nuclear confrontation.

summary: Willy Brandt's Ostpolitik transformed West Germany's relationship with the Eastern bloc, normalising relations and reducing Cold War tensions in Europe.
facts: Ostpolitik (literally 'East Politics') was pursued by West German Chancellor Willy Brandt from 1969. The FRG Hallstein Doctrine had stated that West Germany would break off diplomatic relations with any state that officially recognised the DDR. Brandt saw this as unsustainable — Germany could not be so relentlessly divided.
Brandt signed the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty in 1969. He then began a series of complex treaties with the USSR, Poland, Czechoslovakia and the DDR.

The Moscow Treaty (August 1970) between Brandt and Brezhnev: neither had any territorial claim against any other state; it recognised the western frontier of Poland; Germany finally accepted the loss of territory of 1945 as 'inviolable'; the Federal Republic abandoned the Hallstein Doctrine and agreed both Germanies would become members of the UN.

A treaty with Poland was signed in December 1970 — ethnic Germans still in Poland were to be allowed to emigrate to the West and there were to be more trade links. A treaty with Czechoslovakia was signed in 1973, formally revoking the 1938 Munich Treaty. The Basic Treaty (December 1972) saw the FRG recognise the DDR as an equal sovereign state.
In September 1971, it was agreed that there should be no restrictions on travel between the Federal Republic and West Berlin, and that West Berliners had a right to visit East Berlin.

Brandt won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1971. Ostpolitik gained concessions for West Berlin and had not weakened its ties with the USA or NATO. The way was left open for some future reunification — which came in 1990. However the DDR had gained recognition of its frontiers and there was no suggestion that the internal policies of the DDR should change.

heading: The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan
summary: The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in December 1979 ended détente and began a costly ten-year war that exposed the weaknesses of the Red Army.
facts: In 1978 a communist revolutionary party (the PDPA) had seized power in Afghanistan. Many Afghans rejected the communist government because its atheism was at odds with their Muslim faith — the communists imprisoned, tortured and murdered many Muslim religious leaders. This led to the formation of an anti-communist resistance movement known as the Mujahedeen.

To support the communists, Brezhnev invaded Afghanistan on Christmas Day 1979 with 100,000 Soviet forces. They faced opposition inspired by Islamic beliefs and supported by the USA via Pakistan. Soviet troops withdrew in 1989 after a 10-year war.

The problems of the war: the terrain led to a sustained guerrilla war echoing the US struggle in Vietnam. The opposition fighters had the support of local populations. The war damaged the reputation of the USSR not only in the West but also within the Soviet bloc — over 38,000 Soviets died or were wounded.

The war eroded the confidence of Soviet leaders in using military intervention. Previously, armed Soviet intervention in satellite states had been effective and short-lived. Afghanistan showed this was not always true — and military action was not seen as a viable option in 1989 when the Soviet Empire began to disintegrate.

The war also weakened the Red Army's reputation — its inability to defeat guerrilla forces, the increasing resort to brutality, and the disintegration of discipline and morale combined to undermine the assumption of a great Soviet military machine capable of invading Europe.

The losses in Afghanistan increased resentment within the USSR from non-Russians, who felt they were paying the price for involvement in a war that brought little benefit outside Russia. Protests about the call-up of troops from the Baltic republics grew. 'Draft dodging' became common. When glasnost allowed press freedom, the reporting of the war brought about discontent and demand for political change.

heading: The new Cold War 1979–1984
summary: The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan ended détente and triggered a new period of intense superpower rivalry characterised by Reagan's military build-up and mutual hostility.
facts: America was alarmed at Soviet involvement near the Persian Gulf (threatening US oil interests). President Carter issued the Carter Doctrine — stating that America would respond strongly to any attempts to take control of the Persian Gulf. Carter supplied the Mujahedeen via Pakistan with arms and money.

Economic sanctions on the USSR followed the Afghanistan invasion — Carter ended the US grain trade with the USSR. America refused to attend the 1980 Moscow Olympics; in retaliation the USSR refused to attend the 1984 Los Angeles Olympics.

Ronald Reagan took office in January 1981 with a far more aggressive anti-Soviet stance. He described the USSR as an 'evil empire' and dramatically increased US military spending — raising defence spending from $171 billion in 1981 to $376 billion in 1986.

Reagan developed the Strategic Defence Initiative (SDI — 'Star Wars') in 1983 — a space-based laser defence system designed to intercept Soviet ICBMs. This threatened to make all Soviet nuclear missiles obsolete, and the USSR could not afford to develop a comparable system.

Reagan also stationed Pershing and Cruise missiles in Western Europe in 1983 in response to Soviet SS-20 missiles — causing widespread anti-nuclear protests across Western Europe (the 'peace movement').

unit: Chapter 4 – The End of the Cold War 1984–1995
heading: Problems facing the USSR in the 1980s
summary: By the mid-1980s the USSR faced a deep structural economic crisis compounded by the costs of the arms race, Afghanistan and the Chernobyl disaster.
facts: Brezhnev's rule had been marked by the 'era of stagnation' — the Soviet economy was failing. The Soviet Union had tried to keep up with the USA in the arms race but could not afford to do so. Between 1970 and 1982 defence spending was 15-17% of GDP.
The war in Afghanistan was costing vast amounts of money with no results — over 38,000 Soviets died or were wounded. It eroded the confidence of Soviet leaders in using military intervention.

In 1986 the Chernobyl nuclear power station exploded — $18 billion was spent on containment. The disaster exposed the inefficiency and corruption of Soviet industry and the dangers of the Soviet economic system.

Poor living standards and lack of human rights was causing unrest in the satellite states — for example Solidarity in Poland in 1981. The USSR's declining economy meant it could not meet the consumer demands of its own people or its satellite states.

The two elderly leaders who followed Brezhnev — Yuri Andropov and Konstantin Chernenko — had meant that stagnation characterised policy at a vital time. When Gorbachev became leader in 1985 at the relatively young age of 54, there was widespread understanding in party circles that severe economic problems existed and radical change was needed.

The arms race was also a major factor — Reagan's Strategic Defence Initiative (Star Wars) threatened to make all Soviet ICBMs obsolete. The USSR could not afford to compete with this new technology. Its economy was stagnant and its technology had not kept up with that of the West.

unit: Chapter 4 – The End of the Cold War 1984–1995
heading: Gorbachev — perestroika and glasnost
summary: Gorbachev's twin reforms of perestroika and glasnost were intended to revitalise the USSR — but instead unleashed forces that would destroy it.
facts: Perestroika ('restructuring') referred to the restructuring of the economy — relaxing centralised control and permitting greater economic freedom and initiative. In June 1987, private enterprise was allowed in some industries. However the changes did not lead to grateful appreciation — new private industries did not all prove efficient and long-term economic problems continued. There were more shortages than before of some goods.

Glasnost ('openness') was an 'openness' that would allow more discussion of economic and political issues to drive progress. In 1986 state controls of the media were relaxed and the public learnt about the inefficiencies and corruption that had come to characterise national and local political and economic management.

Political change: in January 1987 Gorbachev spoke openly to the Central Committee of the weaknesses of the system and proposed much greater public participation. Multi-candidate elections by secret ballot for local councils were proposed. In February 1989 there were elections for a new Congress of People's Deputies, which saw the defeat of many of the party establishment. New political leaders from outside the party emerged — including Boris Yeltsin.

The Sinatra Doctrine (1988): Gorbachev replaced the Brezhnev Doctrine with the 'Sinatra Doctrine' — satellite states were now free to 'do it their way'. This was aimed at easing Soviet military spending and avoiding hypocrisy but severely undermined Soviet control in Europe.

The changes divided the Communist Party. Some hardliners felt this was a dangerous path — the threat from the USA and China was unresolved. Others wanted more radical reforms. The hold of the Communist Party began to weaken and new political organisations began to form.

By 1989, Gorbachev would not bolster unpopular communist regimes that were unwilling to apply the remedies he had introduced in the USSR. Thus, integral changes in the USSR paved the way for a new détente — and meant that instead of pressure for change being dictated by Western pressure, it was coming from the leadership of the USSR itself.

unit: Chapter 4 – The End of the Cold War 1984–1995
heading: Reagan, the arms race and Western pressure
summary: Reagan's aggressive military build-up and Strategic Defence Initiative put enormous pressure on the USSR's already failing economy — though Gorbachev's internal reforms were equally important in ending the Cold War.
facts: The new Republican administration of Ronald Reagan was suspicious of the USSR and concerned about the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan and the expansion of Soviet naval forces. Reagan increased US military spending and extended the arms race. He rejected the previous restrictions on defence systems.

With the development of highly sophisticated and expensive new laser and space-based systems (the Strategic Defence Initiative — 'Star Wars'), there was the possibility that the USA could actually win a future conflict. This put the USSR at a disadvantage as its economy was stagnant and its technology had not kept up.

Reagan also fought communist influence in the developing world — supporting anti-communist forces in Nicaragua and invading Grenada. The aid to insurgents in Afghanistan, however, was more serious — it contributed to the Soviet decision that the war was unwinnable.

However, the pressure of the arms race must be kept in perspective. Soviet military spending was already high and did not increase in response to the arms race. The problem was that economic growth was falling and there was a shortage of oil — it was this rather than just pressure from the West that led Gorbachev to seek a way to scale back the arms race.

Reagan and Gorbachev met at Reykjavik in 1986 — Gorbachev attempted to persuade Reagan to give up the SDI developments. Though this failed, Gorbachev succeeded in getting the total withdrawal of medium-range missiles in Europe at a conference between the USSR and NATO in Washington in 1987 — the INF Treaty.

The new détente of 1985–88 was an indication that the USSR was susceptible to pressure. It is possible that the main driving force was the internal situation in the USSR and its republics and satellites — but Western influence and the arms race were a contributory factor.

unit: Chapter 4 – The End of the Cold War 1984–1995
heading: The revolutions of 1989
summary: In 1989, communist regimes across Eastern Europe collapsed in rapid succession — the result of accumulated internal discontent, economic failure and Gorbachev's refusal to use force.
facts: Common elements in the events of 1989: a build-up of resentment against a background of economic underperformance and rising prices; reforming leaders and groups ready to share power; acceptance by Gorbachev and Moscow that states outside the USSR should make changes; widespread popular support for change; rapid arrangements for free elections.

Poland: economic unrest including strikes in the shipyards of Gdansk in 1988 led the government to recognise the Solidarity movement. In April 1989 Round Table Agreements saw Solidarity recognised as a political party. The elections of June 1989 resulted in a Solidarity government — the first non-communist government in Eastern Europe since 1948.

Hungary: unrest in 1988 resulted in the replacement of Kadar by a reforming communist. In 1989 Hungary agreed to hold free elections and opened its borders with Austria in August — this made it possible for 150,000 East Germans to leave for the West via this route.

The DDR: Hungary's open borders triggered demonstrations in Leipzig in September and October 1989. The East German leader Honecker could not count on Gorbachev — who advised him to make changes. The government allowed free exit from 10 November 1989 — and as soon as this was announced, border guards opened up crossing points from East to West Berlin, effectively opening the Berlin Wall. The Wall was subsequently torn down by crowds.

Czechoslovakia — the Velvet Revolution: news from Berlin led to large-scale demonstrations. Opposition groups including Charter 77, led by the dramatist Vaclav Havel, formed Civic Forum. In December a coalition government was formed in which communists were only a minority — Havel was made president. This led to the peaceful end of communism and the formation of Slovakia and the Czech Republic in 1992.

Romania: the only violent revolution. Demonstrations against President Ceausescu began in November 1989 — Ceausescu and his wife fled but were captured and executed on 25 December 1989 — the only leaders to suffer this fate.

unit: Chapter 4 – The End of the Cold War 1984–1995
heading: The fall of the Berlin Wall
summary: The fall of the Berlin Wall on 9 November 1989 was the defining moment of the end of the Cold War — a symbol of communist failure and the triumph of popular pressure.
facts: The Berlin Wall had been built in 1961 to stop the 'brain drain' of East Germans fleeing to the West. By 1989, Hungary's decision to open its borders with Austria had allowed 150,000 East Germans to leave via Hungary. This triggered growing demonstrations in East German cities, especially Leipzig.

The East German leader Honecker was unable to rely on Soviet support — Gorbachev had made clear he would not use force to maintain communist regimes. Honecker was replaced by the reforming communist Egon Krenz.

On 9 November 1989 the government announced that East Germans would be allowed to travel freely. As soon as this was announced, border guards — overwhelmed by crowds — opened up crossing points. Crowds began demolishing the Wall with hammers and pickaxes. The Wall was subsequently torn down.

Reunification brought major problems: confusion about property rights (over 2 million claims filed); East German production costs were very high; links to the collapsing socialist economies of the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe meant East German factories could no longer sell their goods. unit: Chapter 4 – The End of the Cold War 1984–1995
heading: German reunification
summary: German reunification on 3 October 1990 was the defining consequence of the Cold War's end in Europe — achieved rapidly but with enormous economic challenges.
facts: German reunification (3 October 1990) was achieved with remarkable speed under Chancellor Helmut Kohl, who feared a window of opportunity might close. The 'Two Plus Four Treaty' — between the two Germanies and the four wartime Allies — formally recognised reunification and settled the borders of the new state.

On 1 July 1990 the economies of the two Germanies became one — the first time in history that a capitalist and a socialist economy had suddenly merged. The West German Deutschmark replaced the East German Mark at a 1:1 exchange rate, which was economically generous to East Germans but made East German industry instantly uncompetitive.

Reunification brought major structural challenges: East German production costs were very high; links to the collapsing Soviet-bloc economies meant East German factories lost their markets overnight; massive confusion about property rights from successive waves of Nazi, Soviet and GDR expropriations meant over 2 million claims were filed by the December 1992 deadline.

West German investment in the East was enormous — hundreds of billions of Deutschmarks were transferred in the years after reunification. However unemployment in the East rose sharply as uncompetitive factories closed. Many East Germans felt like second-class citizens in the new unified Germany — a phenomenon described as the 'wall in the head'.

France and the USSR were initially unhappy about German reunification — both feared a powerful unified Germany. Gorbachev eventually agreed in return for assurances that NATO would not expand eastwards beyond Germany — an assurance that would become highly controversial in later decades.

Reunification was undoubtedly a triumph for West German diplomacy and for the West's Cold War strategy. It was also a vindication of the Ostpolitik pursued by Willy Brandt — the patient normalisation of relations with the East had laid the groundwork for the peaceful unification that followed.

heading: The coup of 1991 and collapse of the USSR
summary: Gorbachev's reforms had unleashed forces — nationalist movements in Soviet republics and hardline communist opposition — that culminated in a coup attempt and the final collapse of the USSR.
facts: Whilst Gorbachev was seen as a hero in the West (awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1990), in the USSR he was seen as weak. The constituent republics of the USSR saw how easily the satellite states had gained their independence and began to demand the same.
In 1990, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania declared independence from the USSR. Other constituent republics began to follow suit — including Russia, the largest republic, led by Boris Yeltsin.

Gorbachev was increasingly unpopular in Moscow, especially amongst hard-line Communists. In August 1991 eight communist leaders organised a coup and removed Gorbachev from power. They removed glasnost and perestroika.

However Boris Yeltsin led the resistance — standing on a tank outside the Russian Parliament, he rallied popular opposition to the coup. The coup collapsed after just 3 days, restoring Gorbachev to power. But the affair demonstrated how little power Gorbachev had now — Yeltsin acted like he was in control and Gorbachev was just his puppet.

Christmas Day 1991: to avoid a civil war, Gorbachev resigned and announced the breakup of the USSR. The Soviet flag was lowered over the Kremlin and replaced by the Russian flag. Yeltsin became the 1st president of Russia — turning it capitalist.

subheadings.label: The coup
facts: Whilst Gorbachev was seen as a hero in the West (awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1990), in the USSR he was seen as weak. The constituent republics of the USSR saw how easily the satellite states had gained their independence and began to demand the same.
In 1990, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania declared independence from the USSR. Other constituent republics began to follow suit — including Russia, the largest republic, led by Boris Yeltsin.

Gorbachev was increasingly unpopular in Moscow, especially amongst hard-line Communists. In August 1991 eight communist leaders organised a coup and removed Gorbachev from power. They removed glasnost and perestroika.

subheadings.label: Why it failed
facts: However Boris Yeltsin led the resistance — standing on a tank outside the Russian Parliament, he rallied popular opposition to the coup. The coup collapsed after just 3 days, restoring Gorbachev to power. But the affair demonstrated how little power Gorbachev had now — Yeltsin acted like he was in control and Gorbachev was just his puppet.

unit: Chapter 4 – The End of the Cold War 1984–1995
heading: Russia under Yeltsin
summary: Boris Yeltsin's Russia faced enormous challenges in transitioning from communism to capitalism — economic chaos, political instability and the loss of superpower status.
facts: Boris Yeltsin became the first president of the Russian Federation after Gorbachev resigned on Christmas Day 1991. He had been elected president of Russia in June 1991 with 57% of the vote — the first democratic election in Russian history.

Yeltsin introduced 'shock therapy' — a rapid transition to a market economy. Price controls were removed overnight in January 1992, causing hyperinflation. The rouble lost most of its value. Many Russians saw their savings wiped out and living standards collapse.

State industries were privatised rapidly — but the process was corrupt. A small group of well-connected businessmen (the 'oligarchs') acquired vast state assets at far below their true value, becoming billionaires overnight while ordinary Russians suffered.

Yeltsin faced political instability at home. In October 1993, hard-line communist opponents of reform barricaded themselves in the Russian parliament (the 'White House'). Yeltsin ordered tanks to shell the building — at least 187 people were killed. This was the most violent political confrontation in Moscow since the Bolshevik Revolution.

In December 1994 Yeltsin launched a military campaign to prevent the breakaway republic of Chechnya from gaining independence. Russian forces suffered humiliating defeats against Chechen guerrillas. The war cost thousands of lives and further damaged Yeltsin's reputation.

By the mid-1990s Yeltsin's health was failing and his public appearances were frequently embarrassing. Russia had lost its superpower status, its economy was in crisis, and its international influence was a fraction of the USSR's. Yeltsin resigned on 31 December 1999, handing power to his chosen successor — Vladimir Putin.

unit: Chapter 4 – The End of the Cold War 1984–1995
heading: The collapse of Yugoslavia
summary: Yugoslavia's collapse into civil war after communism's fall showed how ethnic and religious tensions suppressed by communist rule could produce catastrophic violence.
facts: Yugoslavia had been a unique communist state — Tito had resisted Stalin and maintained independence. It was a federation of six republics and two autonomous regions with a complex ethnic and religious mix. Tito's death in 1980 removed the one figure who had held the federation together.

Serbian nationalist Slobodan Milosevic became president of Serbia in 1989 and promoted the interests of Serbs across Yugoslavia. This fuelled nationalist movements in Slovenia and Croatia, which declared independence in June 1991. War broke out immediately — the Yugoslav People's Army (largely Serbian-controlled) fought the breakaway republics.

In Bosnia, a three-way conflict between Bosnian Muslims, Bosnian Serbs and Bosnian Croats led to the worst violence in Europe since WWII. Serbian forces conducted 'ethnic cleansing' — massacring or expelling Bosnian Muslims from their homes. The Srebrenica massacre of July 1995 saw 8,000 Bosnian Muslim men and boys murdered.

The international community was slow to respond. The UN deployed peacekeepers who lacked the mandate to stop the killing. The USA and NATO eventually intervened — NATO bombing campaigns against Serb positions in Bosnia in 1995 forced the Dayton Peace Agreement.

In Kosovo (1999), NATO launched a 78-day air campaign against Serbia after Milosevic launched a campaign of ethnic cleansing against Kosovar Albanians. Serbian forces withdrew from Kosovo, which remained technically part of Serbia under UN administration.

Religion mobilised ethnic elimination of minority groups — Orthodox Christianity, Catholicism and Islam all reinforced old stereotypes and nationalist identities. The Yugoslav wars showed the dangerous consequences of communism's fall in multi-ethnic states — when the communist framework suppressing ethnic nationalism was removed, old rivalries re-emerged with catastrophic force.
